target.title: fix(microsoft-foundry): bound az subprocess lifetime on exec timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`execFileSync` default `killSignal` is `SIGTERM`. When the Azure CLI (`az`) hits a network stall during token acquisition, it may ignore `SIGTERM` and block the gateway thread past the 30s timeout — leaving the sync call path hung with no recovery.

## Why This Change Was Made

Adding `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` to the `execFileSync` call ensures the `az` subprocess is forcefully terminated when the 30s timeout fires.

The async counterpart `execAzAsync` calls `runExec` (from `openclaw/plugin-sdk/process-runtime`), not the Node.js built-in `execFile`. `runExec` delegates to execa with `forceKillAfterDelay: COMMAND_PROCESS_TREE_KILL_GRACE_MS` (300ms), providing a built-in two-phase kill: `SIGTERM` → 300ms grace → `SIGKILL`. Source: `src/process/exec.ts:50-63`, `src/process/exec-spawn.ts:7`.

## Evidence Map

| Layer | Detail |
|-------|--------|
| **Changed surface** | `execAz` in `extensions/microsoft-foundry/cli.ts:47-58` — one line |
| **Node.js contract** | `execFileSync` default `killSignal` is `SIGTERM` (Node.js docs); no force-kill fallback on timeout |
| **Callers** | `isAzCliInstalled:77`, `getLoggedInAccount:86`, `listSubscriptions:95`, `getAccessTokenResult:135` — all sync, all on gateway hot paths |
| **Sibling** | `execAzAsync:60-73` uses `runExec` (`src/process/exec.ts:50-63`) with built-in `SIGTERM` → 300ms → `SIGKILL` — already safe |
| **Mock test** | `index.test.ts:591` — verifies `execFileSyncMock` receives `killSignal: "SIGKILL"` |
| **Behavioral proof (sync)** | `index.test.ts:604` — spawns real Node process ignoring `SIGTERM`, confirms `SIGKILL` terminates it within 2s |
| **Behavioral proof (async)** | `index.test.ts:622` — spawns real Node process via `runExec`, confirms two-phase kill (SIGTERM → SIGKILL) terminates within 2s |
| **Test suite** | 96/96 pass |

## User Impact

- Prevents hung `az` processes from blocking gateway sync operations
- No behavioral change for successful `az` invocations
- 30s timeout, encoding, and all other options unchanged

target.title: fix(sms): isolate validated webhook quotas per sender
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The SMS webhook's accepted-callback quota was keyed by resolved client address. Twilio shares egress addresses across unrelated senders, so one flooding sender could exhaust the 30/minute callback budget and make valid callbacks from other users fail with HTTP 429.

## Why This Change Was Made

The patch keeps the existing pre-validation failed-request budget keyed by account, route, and client address, but moves the post-validation dispatch quota to account, route, and canonical sender identity.

- Signature-validated callbacks use `resolveTwilioInboundSender(form)`, so equivalent SMS and `RCS:` address forms share one sender bucket.
- A true single-sender overload remains observable as HTTP 429; the handler does not acknowledge and silently discard it.
- Another validated sender behind the same Twilio egress address remains dispatchable.
- With `dangerouslyDisableSignatureValidation`, `From` is unauthenticated, so the stricter callback budget stays keyed to the resolved client address and cannot be bypassed by rotating sender text.

## User Impact

One abusive or bursty sender can no longer cross-throttle unrelated SMS users behind Twilio's shared infrastructure. Existing thresholds and invalid-request behavior remain unchanged, while genuine overload remains fail-closed and visible.

Accepted tradeoff: removing the accidental aggregate egress-IP cap means many distinct signature-validated senders can each use their own 30/minute budget. That is intentional sender isolation; downstream pairing/access policy remains the authorization boundary.

## Evidence

Current contributor head: `16bdfc604bd` on upstream `main` `0483001ef65`.

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/sms/src/webhook.test.ts`: focused suite passed, including the new quota-isolation regressions.
- Positive regression: 30 callbacks from sender A are accepted; sender B on the same egress address is still accepted.
- Negative regression: sender A's 31st callback returns 429 even when its address changes from SMS E.164 syntax to equivalent `RCS:+1 (555) 123-4567` syntax and even when the egress IP changes.
- Signature-disabled regression: rotating `From` values does not widen the address-keyed quota.
- Invalid/missing canonical senders share an empty-sender bucket without consuming a valid sender's quota.
- Fixed-window recovery regression: the sender becomes dispatchable after the window expires.
- Direct formatter check and `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD` passed.
- The pre-PR plan gate passed for extension, extension-test, and docs lanes with no dependency-sensitive changes.

### Real behavior proof

The focused suite drives the real request-body parser, Twilio HMAC validation, canonical sender resolver, fixed-window limiter, response writer, and durable-ingress seam with realistic HTTP requests. It proves both the intended isolation and the closest bypasses without deploying the Gateway.

No live Twilio callback was sent to this exact branch head, and no Gateway restart or production webhook change was performed. A maintainer-controlled live Twilio smoke remains the strongest optional transport proof.

AI-assisted; reviewed and validated before submission.

target.title: fix(qa-lab): bound internal transport response reads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where QA Lab runs could buffer arbitrarily large internal adapter responses or remain stuck after response headers when a Crabline adapter or runtime-parity debug endpoint returned an oversized or stalled JSON body.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both QA Lab-owned response readers now use the public plugin SDK response-limit seam with a 1 MiB cap, a 5-second idle deadline, and a 15-second overall body deadline. Crabline keeps failing the injection on invalid transport responses, while runtime parity keeps its existing fail-soft behavior and treats unavailable mock request data as absent; normal provider message IDs and parity ordering are unchanged.

## User Impact

QA operators get bounded failure instead of memory growth or an indefinitely stalled suite when an internal transport endpoint misbehaves. Healthy Telegram, Slack, Matrix, and runtime-parity responses continue through the same workflows.

## Evidence

AI-assisted.

### Real behavior proof

Environment: local Linux machine, Node `v24.18.0`, exact base `b8b064a9483ee0917648207ffe91438a2da8c828`. A real localhost HTTP server streamed either 2 MiB of JSON in 64 KiB chunks or sent a JSON prefix and then stalled. The harness loaded the production `postCrablineInbound` and `captureRuntimeParityCell` callers from an isolated main worktree and this branch. Main's private Crabline caller received a proof-only export in the isolated worktree; its implementation was unchanged.

Command (run once against main and once against this branch):

```text
node --import tsx /tmp/openclaw-qa-response-proof.mjs \
  <worktree>/extensions/qa-lab/src/crabline-transport.ts \
  <worktree>/extensions/qa-lab/src/runtime-parity.ts
```

Before (`upstream/main`):

```json
{"surface":"crabline","mode":"oversized","outcome":"resolved","elapsedMs":240,"bytesWritten":2097166}
{"surface":"runtime-parity","mode":"oversized","outcome":"resolved","elapsedMs":223,"bytesWritten":2097166}
{"surface":"crabline","mode":"stalled","outcome":"observer-timeout","elapsedMs":6501,"bytesWritten":11}
{"surface":"runtime-parity","mode":"stalled","outcome":"observer-timeout","elapsedMs":6501,"bytesWritten":11}
```

Premise: both main callers consumed the complete 2 MiB response. After only 11 bytes of a stalled JSON body, neither caller completed within the harness's 6.5-second observer deadline; the guarded fetch had already resolved on headers.

After (this branch):

```json
{"surface":"crabline","mode":"oversized","outcome":"rejected:Crabline inbound response exceeds 1048576 bytes","elapsedMs":153,"bytesWritten":1114124}
{"surface":"runtime-parity","mode":"oversized","outcome":"resolved","elapsedMs":130,"bytesWritten":1048588}
{"surface":"crabline","mode":"stalled","outcome":"rejected:Media download stalled: no data received for 5000ms","elapsedMs":5005,"bytesWritten":11,"closedBeforeEnd":true}
{"surface":"runtime-parity","mode":"stalled","outcome":"resolved","elapsedMs":5004,"bytesWritten":11,"closedBeforeEnd":true}
```

The Crabline caller now fails at the byte/idle boundary. Runtime parity still resolves fail-soft, but stops reading at the same boundaries. Both stalled connections were canceled before the server ended the body.

Negative controls: the same production paths' existing healthy-response tests remained green, including normal Telegram/Slack/Matrix provider message IDs and normal runtime-parity request ordering.

target.title: Bound trajectory pointer file read with size cap
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readTrajectoryPointerFile` calls `fs.readFileSync(pointerPath, "utf8")` on session trajectory pointer files with no size limit. A corrupted pointer file can OOM the trajectory cleanup path.

## Why This Change Was Made

PR #101472 established the bounded-read pattern for file reads. Trajectory pointer files are small JSON metadata files, but the unbounded `readFileSync` call was a latent vulnerability. Using `readRegularFileSync` with a 1 MB cap (generous for pointer files which are typically <1 KB) prevents OOM from corrupted pointer files.

## User Impact

No user-visible change. Trajectory pointer files are small JSON objects (<1 KB typically); a 1 MB cap is more than sufficient. Corrupted oversized pointer files gracefully return `null` (already handled by the existing try-catch).

## Evidence

- Replaced `fs.readFileSync(pointerPath, "utf8")` with `readRegularFileSync({ filePath: pointerPath, maxBytes: TRAJECTORY_POINTER_MAX_BYTES })` at `src/trajectory/cleanup.ts:65-69`
- Added `TRAJECTORY_POINTER_MAX_BYTES = 1 * 1024 * 1024` constant
- Added `readRegularFileSync` import from `../infra/regular-file.js`

target.title: fix(qa-lab): unref detached qa cli child and detach stdio listeners
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`runQaCli` in `extensions/qa-lab/src/suite-runtime-agent-process.ts` spawns the QA CLI as a detached child and attaches `data` listeners to its `stdout`/`stderr`, but never removed them. After the child closed, the retained listeners kept the stream references alive longer than necessary — a child-process lifecycle cleanup gap.

## Why This Change Was Made

On `close`, detach both stdio `data` listeners (`child.stdout.off("data", onStdout)` / `child.stderr.off("data", onStderr)`). The handlers are named functions so the exact references can be removed. An earlier unconditional `child.unref()` was dropped per review feedback (ineffective for the cleanup goal); the close-time detachment is the retained behavior.

## User Impact

No behavior change for QA suite runs; the parent process no longer retains stdio listeners after the QA CLI child closes.

## Real behavior proof — actual detached QA CLI child run (final head, 2026-07-19)

The exported `runQaCli` was invoked directly on the PR head. It spawned a **real detached subprocess** (`node <repoRoot>/dist/index.js ...`, production spawn path with `detached: true`, piped stdio); a stub CLI stands in for the openclaw entry so the scenario is hermetic — spawn, streams, close handling, and listener cleanup are all the production code path.

```bash
time ./node_modules/.bin/tsx child-lifecycle-proof.mts
```

```text

node: v24.18.0
code path: extensions/qa-lab/src/suite-runtime-agent-process.ts runQaCli (real detached spawn)
[success] runQaCli resolved in 52ms: {"ok":true,"argv":["memory","status","--json"]}
[failure] rejected in 46ms: qa cli failed (2): boom
[cleanup] active handles after close: Socket, Socket, Socket, ChildProcess
[cleanup] parent's own stdio Sockets plus the already-closed ChildProcess object are expected;
```

Fixes an issue where operators using Microsoft Teams federated authentication could have whitespace-only certificate settings reported as configured. Gateway startup would then try to read a certificate file whose path consisted only of spaces instead of treating the certificate credential as missing.

## Why This Change Was Made

Federated certificate paths, thumbprints, and managed-identity client IDs now use one owner-local string normalizer for config-over-environment resolution. This keeps blank config values from shadowing valid environment values while leaving secret authentication and managed-identity selection unchanged.

## User Impact

Microsoft Teams setup and status now reject blank certificate configuration consistently, and a blank config field can correctly fall back to a valid trimmed environment setting.

AI-assisted.

## Evidence

Local-machine production-function proof on Node `v24.18.0`:

1. **Before / negative control against exact latest main `aaa37a0c264a9b2bc25c6d5a8e98ede130455fed`:** in a detached worktree, imported `extensions/msteams/src/token.ts`, set `appId`, `tenantId`, `authType: "federated"`, and whitespace-only config/env certificate fields, then called both exported credential functions.

   ```text
   {"configured":true,"resolved":{"type":"federated","appId":"app-id","tenantId":"tenant-id","certificatePath":"   ","certificateThumbprint":"   "}}
   ```

   This is RED: the production resolver returned federated credentials that `createFederatedApp` passes to `readFileSync`, and channel/setup callers use the resolver result as their configured predicate.

2. **After on final head `ebb41b33145839be4dfda2e8bd4c9c069884f00d`:** ran the same exported production functions first with blank config/env values, then with the same blank config plus padded valid env values.

   ```text
   {"blank":{"configured":false,"resolved":null},"fallback":{"configured":true,"resolved":{"type":"federated","appId":"app-id","tenantId":"tenant-id","certificatePath":"/env/cert.pem","certificateThumbprint":"EEFF0011"}}}
   ```

3. **Focused regression and controls:**

   ```text
   node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/msteams/src/token.test.ts
   Test Files  1 passed (1)
   Tests       22 passed (22)
   ```

   The focused file also keeps valid certificate config/env, secret credentials, system/user managed identity, and explicit `useManagedIdentity=false` behavior covered.

4. `./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/msteams/src/token.ts extensions/msteams/src/token.test.ts` passed; `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD` passed.

5. `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode branch --base upstream/main` completed clean with no accepted/actionable findings (overall patch-correct score `0.96`).

Not tested: a live Microsoft Teams certificate login, because no tenant certificate credentials were available. The changed behavior is entirely before SDK/network dispatch; the proof drives the exported production credential resolver that all channel, setup, probe, graph, monitor, and send-context callers consume.

Fixes an issue where the managed-worktree test suite fails on hosts using a cooperative `0002` umask, even though worktree provisioning correctly preserves the file modes those hosts actually create.

target.title: fix(gateway): keep channel lifecycle outside released request admission
target.body:
Closes #110697

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where channel accounts started or restarted from a short-lived gateway request could stop accepting later work after that request finished. Provider callbacks, approval bootstrap follow-up, and automatic restarts could retain the released request's admission context and fail with `GatewayDrainingError` even though the process-global gateway fence was still open.

## Why This Change Was Made

Channel lifecycle work is process-lifetime, not request-lifetime. The channel manager now creates approval-bootstrap work and the full provider -> cleanup -> auto-restart promise chain outside the current gateway request admission root, using the existing `runOutsideGatewayRootWorkAdmission` helper. Process-global restart and suspension fences remain authoritative; this change only stops a released request root from poisoning long-lived channel tasks.

Compatibility: no config, protocol, or public API change; callers of `createChannelManager` / `startChannel` keep the same surface. Performance: one ALS exit at lifecycle creation, no request-time discovery. Usability: channels stay responsive after the starting RPC/reload ends. Security: does not reopen admission during real drain or suspension.

## User Impact

Long-running channel accounts remain able to accept work after the gateway request or reload that started them has completed. Real process restart and suspension still refuse new work normally.

## Evidence

Exact current head: `a73e8d29d7fbe8e245c0e37f386dc14de8f32b2d`.

- [Full CI run 29649706201](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29649706201): passed on prior head, including all four QA Smoke CI profiles.
- Focused production-patch proof on `ca8722dbbc`: `src/gateway/server-channels.test.ts` 53/53 passed; `src/process/gateway-work-admission.test.ts` 17/17 passed.
- Formatting/lint on the touched production and test files: `oxfmt --check` passed; `oxlint` reported 0 warnings and 0 errors; `git diff --check` clean.
- Isolated QA scenario: `qa/scenarios/channels/channel-lifecycle-admission.yaml`.

New focused cases:

1. `does not inherit a released request admission into a channel task`
2. `does not inherit a released request admission into approval bootstrap work`
3. `does not inherit a released request admission into an automatic channel restart`

## Real behavior proof

Isolated real gateway + `qa-channel` + `mock-openai` run at head `a73e8d29d7` (after the scenario harness fix that drives suspend prepare/resume over Admin HTTP, matching docs for hosts that cannot keep a WebSocket open across suspension).

Command:

```bash
OPENCLAW_BUILD_PRIVATE_QA=1 pnpm openclaw qa suite \
  --provider-mode mock-openai \
  --scenario channel-lifecycle-admission \
  --channel-driver qa-channel \
  --output-dir .artifacts/qa-e2e/channel-lifecycle-admission-proof3
```

Result: **passed=1 failed=0** in ~11s.

Redacted step transcript:

```text
[qa-suite] scenario pass (1/1): channel-lifecycle-admission
[qa-suite] run complete: passed=1 failed=0 skipped=0 total=1

Step 1: accepts channel work after the starting RPC root is released — pass
{
  "stopped": { "channel": "qa-channel", "accountId": "default", "stopped": true },
  "started": { "channel": "qa-channel", "accountId": "default", "started": true },
  "firstOutbound": "QA-CHANNEL-LIFECYCLE-AFTER-RPC-OK"
}

Step 2: preserves process-global suspension refusal and resumes delivery — pass
{
  "suspension": {
    "status": "ready",
    "suspensionId": "424d4adc-…-ce424fc01836",
    "activeCount": 0,
    "blockers": []
  },
  "suspendedCallError": "channels.status unavailable during gateway suspension (reason=gateway-suspending, phase=prepared)",
  "resumed": { "ok": true, "status": "running", "resumed": true },
  "resumedOutbound": "QA-CHANNEL-LIFECYCLE-AFTER-RESUME-OK"
}
```

Observable sequence matched the review acceptance criteria:

1. `channels.stop` / `channels.start` return for the real QA channel account.
2. After the start RPC root is gone, inbound work produces `QA-CHANNEL-LIFECYCLE-AFTER-RPC-OK`.
3. Prepared suspension rejects ordinary `channels.status` with `UNAVAILABLE` / `gateway-suspending`.
4. `gateway.suspend.resume` returns `running`; inbound work then produces `QA-CHANNEL-LIFECYCLE-AFTER-RESUME-OK`.

Scenario note: suite `gateway.call` opens a new WebSocket per RPC, and a prepared suspension rejects new handshakes by design (`docs/gateway/external-apps.md`). The scenario therefore enables the bundled `admin-http-rpc` plugin for prepare / refuse / resume control while still exercising the real channel delivery path on qa-channel.

target.title: fix(acp): /acp sessions exposes every gateway session to non-owner senders
target.body:
Closes #103055

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an authorized non-owner sender could run `/acp sessions` and enumerate every ACP session on the Gateway, including session keys, labels, agents, runtime state, backend, and thread bindings belonging to other senders or the owner.

## Why This Change Was Made

`/acp sessions` now enforces visibility at the command boundary, where sender authorization and the current conversation binding are available. Owners and internal `operator.admin` clients retain the full diagnostic listing. Other authorized senders perform a targeted read of only their current bound or requester session, and that result is included only when both the stored session entry and ACP metadata exist.

The shared session registry remains gateway-wide because startup identity reconciliation and task maintenance legitimately need to scan every ACP session. Explicit target tokens are rejected by `/acp sessions`, preventing callers from redirecting this read to another session. Bound-thread resolution continues to take precedence over the raw requester session key.

Sibling read-only actions were checked: `doctor` and `install` expose backend health or setup instructions but do not enumerate session identifiers. The `/acp sessions` path does not log session identifiers.

Release-note context: authorized non-owner senders and internal `operator.write` clients no longer see Gateway-wide ACP sessions; they see only their current ACP session. Owners and `operator.admin` clients retain the full listing.

## User Impact

Authorized non-owner senders can still use `/acp sessions` for their current ACP session without learning about other users' sessions. Owners and administrative Gateway clients keep the aggregate diagnostic view.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/auto-reply/reply/commands-acp.test.ts`: 73 passed. The matrix covers owner-wide visibility, internal `operator.admin` visibility, scoped `operator.write`, non-owner current raw ACP sessions, bound-thread precedence, ordinary non-ACP requester sessions, missing requester keys, and explicit foreign target rejection.
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check docs/tools/acp-agents.md src/auto-reply/reply/commands-acp.test.ts src/auto-reply/reply/commands-acp/diagnostics.ts`: passed.

target.title: fix(oc-path): reject oversized multibyte JSONC input

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running OC Path against JSONC input above the 16 MiB byte cap could receive normal empty or not-found output instead of a typed size rejection. Multibyte input could also bypass the intended byte cap because the parser measured UTF-16 code units.

## Why This Change Was Made

The shared JSONC parser now measures UTF-8 bytes before the empty-input shortcut and `parseTree`. The OC Path CLI loader propagates the existing `OC_JSONC_INPUT_TOO_LARGE` diagnostic through its structured parse-error path for every verb that loads JSON/JSONC, without changing other parser-warning behavior or adding another limit.

## User Impact

OC Path now consistently rejects oversized multibyte and whitespace-only JSONC before allocating the parse tree, and CLI callers receive the documented machine-readable parse-error diagnostic instead of a misleading normal result.

target.title: fix(cli): bound dns-cli subprocess probes with timeout
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The `brew --prefix` capability probe in `dns-cli.ts` uses `spawnSync` without a timeout. A hung DNS tool shim can block `openclaw dns setup --apply` indefinitely before setup even starts.

## Why This Change Was Made

Prevents indefinite hangs from a misbehaving `brew` probe during DNS setup, without changing the behavior of legitimate long-running setup steps.

## User Impact

No functional change for normal setups. The `brew --prefix` probe is now bounded by a 15s SIGKILL-backed deadline, so a hung (even signal-resistant) probe terminates and the CLI exits with a clear error instead of blocking forever. Install, service restart, and sudo file-write steps keep their previous unbounded wait.

## Evidence

Real environment: macOS (Darwin 24.6.0 arm64), Node v24.18.0, pnpm 11.2.2. Both runs use a real built CLI (`pnpm install && pnpm build`, launched via `node openclaw.mjs`). A controlled hung `brew` shim (`#!/bin/sh` + `exec sleep 3600`) is placed first on `PATH`, so `dns setup --apply` blocks inside the real `brew --prefix` probe in `run()`. The test machine has no Tailscale, so a `NODE_OPTIONS=--import` preload injects a fake `100.64.0.1` interface entry to pass the command's tailnet-IP gate; that gate is unrelated to this change and no production code was modified for the harness. State is isolated via `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`/`OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH` pointing at a scratch dir.

Exact command:

```sh
node openclaw.mjs dns setup --domain openclaw.internal --apply
```

Before (upstream/main @ 28069db63aa, same harness): the CLI prints the setup plan, then blocks inside the hung probe and never returns; the outer guard kills it after 40s.

```
Tailscale admin (DNS → Nameservers):
- Add nameserver: 100.64.0.1
- Restrict to domain (Split DNS): openclaw.internal
---- result ----
elapsed_seconds=41
exit_code=137
verdict=CLI STILL BLOCKED after 40s guard; killed by harness (unbounded hang)
```

After (this PR @ d41b4ffa10b): the probe's 15s deadline fires, `spawnSync brew ETIMEDOUT` is reported, and the CLI exits with a clear error instead of blocking (~3s CLI startup + 15s timeout = 18s). `ps` afterwards shows no leftover `sleep 3600` process, i.e. SIGKILL reaped the hung probe.

```
Tailscale admin (DNS → Nameservers):
```

target.title: fix(reef): repeated relay reconnects no longer leave stale sockets active
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where a local Reef frame-processing failure could allow a replacement WebSocket generation to start while the abandoned socket was still closing. Repeated failures could therefore overlap stale and replacement sockets and leave stale socket activity during channel shutdown.

## Why This Change Was Made

Each Reef inbox WebSocket generation now owns one terminal transition. A locally failed generation preserves its original error and waits for confirmed close before allowing reconnect. Production `ws` sockets force-terminate after five seconds if the peer does not finish closing, and injected factories must provide the same termination capability; reconnect still waits for the resulting real `close` event. The implementation is rebased onto the current durable-cursor and serialized-recovery lifecycle from `main`, which already removes each generation's abort listener on terminal transition; the regression coverage preserves that existing invariant.

## User Impact

Long-running Reef channels can reconnect repeatedly without overlapping failed and replacement sockets. Channel abort closes the active generation and waits for both its socket and in-flight serialized work to finish.

## Evidence

- Rebased onto pinned `main` (`a7e47653fc8`) and resolved the Reef transport conflict while preserving both the current Relay request deadline and this PR's bounded production WebSocket close.
- Inspected the old-head `check-test-types` failure: both errors came from the two new reconnect tests returning `ControlledSocket` without the existing `WebSocketLike` test-double cast. The rebased head now types both factories consistently; fresh hosted CI will validate the updated head.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts`
  - 1 test file passed
  - 27 tests passed
  - Covers durable recovery plus active-generation listener ownership, malformed-frame error preservation, close-before-reconnect ordering, and forced termination waiting for its asynchronous real close event.
- `./node_modules/.bin/oxfmt --check extensions/reef/src/transport.ts extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts`
  - All matched files use the correct format.
- Fresh near-real network proof used the production `createReefWebSocket` client from the rebased head against a local protocol-compatible WebSocket relay. Redacted event order:

```text
connected:1
sent:malformed-frame
state:connected
state:disconnected
closed:1
error:original-malformed-frame
connected:2
replacement-after-close
state:connected
abort:channel
state:disconnected
closed:2
```

  Assertions passed: two generations observed; failed generation closed before replacement; original malformed-frame failure preserved; final abort closed the replacement; zero relay peers remained.

- A second fresh near-real proof exercised the five-second forced-termination branch with the production real `ws` client and a local relay. Graceful close was deliberately stalled and the underlying `close` event was delayed after `terminate()` returned. The replacement connected only after that delayed close event was forwarded; the original malformed-frame error was preserved, abort closed the replacement, and zero relay peers remained.

### Proof boundary

The live proof uses real `ws` network sockets and the production Reef transport owner, with a local protocol-compatible relay rather than a hosted Reef service. A full gateway startup is not the canonical owner of this ordering: malformed-frame handling, socket close completion, reconnect, and abort cleanup all occur inside `ReefInboxConnection`.

target.title: fix(agents): mid-turn assistant text from claude-cli turns never reaches the channel even with block streaming enabled
target.body:
Closes #110067
Related: #106760

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running agents on the `claude-cli` backend would receive only the final short wrap-up of a multi-tool turn, while the substantive mid-turn assistant text — findings, explanations, and even direct questions to the operator — was silently never delivered to the channel.

The durable channel reply for a CLI-backed turn is the CLI `result` field, which carries only the final assistant message. All earlier completed text blocks reach the gateway in real time, but block streaming (`blockStreamingDefault: "on"` / `*.streaming.block.enabled`) was only wired for the embedded runtime: the CLI dispatch path wires `onAssistantText` into the ephemeral preview lane and pre-tool commentary into the ephemeral progress-draft lane, and nothing feeds the durable block-reply pipeline. The field report in #110067 measured a worst case of 3,221 chars of prose across 7 text blocks reduced to a delivered 373-char final block, with a discarded 1,699-char block containing the actual findings and a question the operator never received. #106760 is the same loss observed through Telegram.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Claude stream-json parser already detects every completed-segment boundary (tool_use `content_block_start`, other `content_block_start`, `message_stop`, terminal `result`); this change adds a completed-segment callback at exactly those existing flush points, tagging each segment with its assistant-message ordinal. Segments ride the existing assistant agent-event stream as `blockText` events — deliberately without `text`/`delta` fields, so every existing consumer (previews, live chat, ws-log, OpenAI-compatible endpoints), which keys on those fields, ignores them; emission is additionally gated on a per-run flag that is only set when a block consumer is wired. A new dispatch bridge delivers the segments through the same `blockReplyHandler` the embedded candidate uses, only when block streaming is enabled for the turn, so all existing gates (silent-run suppression, silent-token stripping, threading, coalescing, pipeline ordering and dedupe) apply unchanged.

The terminal CLI result is deduplicated by the existing final-assembly evidence (`hasSentPayload` exact-content and per-message fragment coverage). One generic gap is closed alongside: the CLI can merge an interim result and a post-notification result into a single terminal payload spanning two assistant messages, which per-message fragment coverage cannot match, so `hasSentPayload` now also compares against all streamed fragments in send order — for per-message finals (the embedded shape) this is unreachable, because any earlier non-empty message makes the full-run concatenation a strict superset of the final message's fragments.

Scope is deliberately bounded to the Claude stream-json dialect: Gemini stream-json and Codex item-based results already fold all streamed text into the terminal result, so those backends have no loss to fix (pinned by a test). Segments deliver at completed-text-block grain in both `blockStreamingBreak` modes; the embedded runtime's flush-before-tool behaves the same way at tool boundaries, which are the dominant CLI segment boundary. The followup queue lane is unchanged: it has no live block lane for the embedded runtime either, and delivers final payloads through `sendRunPayloads` for both runtimes, so runtime parity is preserved there.

## User Impact

With block streaming enabled, agents on `claude-cli` (and any custom `claude-stream-json` CLI backend) now deliver each completed mid-turn text block as a normal durable channel message, exactly as the embedded runtime does and as `docs/concepts/streaming.md` documents. Operators of long multi-tool turns see narration, findings, and questions when they are written instead of losing them; the final wrap-up is not duplicated. Turns with block streaming disabled are unchanged, previews and progress drafts are unchanged, and no config, protocol, or persisted-state shape changes.

## Evidence

### Live behavior proof (production CLI runner, real subprocess, production block pipeline and final assembly)

Driver: the production `runCliAgentWithLifecycle` (real `runCliAgent`, real agent-event bridges) spawns a real child process replaying a protocol-faithful Claude stream-json multi-tool turn (substantive narration + question -> `tool_use` -> tool result -> short wrap-up -> `result` envelope), wired to the production `createBlockReplyDeliveryHandler` + `createBlockReplyPipeline` with block streaming enabled, then through the production `buildReplyPayloads` final assembly. The only substitutions are the channel sink (console logger) and the CLI binary (config-registered stream-json backend pointing at the replay script).

Before (current `main`) — the narration and the question never reach the channel; the only delivered message is the wrap-up:

```
[proof] production CLI runner + fake claude subprocess (claude stream-json)
[agent/cli-backend] cli exec: provider=proof-claude-cli model=default promptChars=48 ...
[agent/cli-backend] cli turn: provider=proof-claude-cli model=default durationMs=1397 ...
[proof] terminal CLI result payload: "Done — config check complete."
[channel] delivered message: "Done — config check complete."
[proof] FINAL: durable channel messages (1) = ["Done — config check complete."]
```

After (this patch) — the completed mid-turn block is delivered durably while the turn runs, and the terminal result is suppressed as already streamed instead of double-delivering:

```
[proof] production CLI runner + fake claude subprocess (claude stream-json)
[agent/cli-backend] cli exec: provider=proof-claude-cli model=default promptChars=48 ...
[channel] delivered message: "I inspected the channel config: the webhook secret is missing and retries are set to 0, which is why deliveries drop. Should I also enable retries while I fix this?"
[channel] delivered message: "Done — config check complete."
[agent/cli-backend] cli turn: provider=proof-claude-cli model=default durationMs=1558 ...
[proof] terminal CLI result payload: "Done — config check complete."
[proof] FINAL: durable channel messages (2) = ["I inspected the channel config: ... Should I also enable retries while I fix this?","Done — config check complete."]
```

### Regression coverage

- `cli-output.test.ts` (6 new): segment emission with message ordinals across tool boundaries; pre-tool segments alongside commentary when both consumers are wired; segment splits at text-block boundaries within one message; tail segment on `result` without `message_stop`; tail segment on truncated streams; no segments for the Gemini dialect.
- `agent-runner-cli-dispatch.test.ts` (2 new): the bridge delivers `blockText` events in order and requests their emission while the snapshot preview lane stays isolated; silent-expected runs suppress block delivery.
- `block-reply-pipeline.test.ts` (1 new): finals that merge several streamed assistant messages are recognized as already sent.
- `agent-runner.misc.runreplyagent.test.ts` (1 new, full `runReplyAgent` integration): completed CLI segments stream as durable block replies and the matching terminal payload is not delivered again.
- Against unfixed `main`, 8 of the 10 new tests fail (the two that pass are the negative-behavior guards: Gemini exclusion and silent-run suppression); all pre-existing tests in the touched files pass unchanged in both states.
- Focused runs on the fix: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs` -> `cli-output.test.ts` 73 passed, `agent-runner-cli-dispatch.test.ts` 24 passed, `block-reply-pipeline.test.ts` 22 passed, `agent-runner.misc.runreplyagent.test.ts` 76 passed, `followup-runner.test.ts` 150 passed, `agent-runner-execution-cli-progress.test.ts` + `agent-runner-execution-cli-sessions.test.ts` 14 passed, `claude-live-session-policy/execute-output-buffer/execute.supervisor-capture` 48 passed.
- `pnpm tsgo:core`, `pnpm tsgo:core:test`, and `pnpm tsgo:test:src` clean; scoped `scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` and `oxfmt` clean on all touched files; `git diff --check` clean.

### Sibling-surface context

The audit behind this fix checked the other decision surfaces for the same defect family: Gemini stream-json and Codex item-dialect terminal results already include all streamed text (no durable loss; the Gemini exclusion is pinned by a test); the embedded runtime path is untouched and its block delivery is unchanged; the followup queue lane runs both runtimes without a live block lane and is intentionally left symmetric; the `claude-stdio` live-session path shares the same streaming parser and receives the same callback plumbing as the plain spawn path; and the ephemeral preview, reasoning, and commentary progress lanes are unchanged, including their existing gating.

target.title: fix(polls): add default maximum poll option count
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Matrix polls would accept more than 20 options despite the Matrix MSC3381 protocol capping poll options at 20. Unlike other channels (Discord=10, WhatsApp=12, MS Teams=12, Telegram=12), the Matrix channel did not enforce its protocol limit, potentially causing protocol violations when sending polls with more than 20 options.

## Why This Change Was Made

Enforce the MSC3381 20-option limit at the Matrix boundary by truncating oversized poll inputs in `buildPollStartContent`. The implementation:
- Truncates options > 20 to the first 20 options (keeps the channel operational for oversized inputs)
- Preserves the shared `normalizePollInput` helper's public contract (omitted `maxOptions` = no limit)
- Avoids adapter-level validation that would interfere with Matrix builder truncation

The truncation approach was chosen per reviewer feedback to ensure existing callers with > 20 options still produce valid `m.poll.start` events instead of failing closed.

## User Impact

Matrix poll senders can now:
- Send polls with up to 20 options (accepted as-is)
- Send polls with > 20 options (truncated to first 20, channel remains operational)
- Other channels and shared poll utilities remain unchanged

No user-visible breaking changes; oversized polls now produce valid Matrix events instead of potentially violating protocol.

## Evidence

### Behavioral tests at the Matrix builder boundary (head `a1281442` (rebased onto latest main))

```bash
pnpm vitest run extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.test.ts src/polls.test.ts
```

```text
Test Files  2 passed (2)
     Tests  17 passed (17)
```

Covered behavior:
- **20 options:** builder accepts and preserves all 20 options; emits 20 `m.poll.start` answers
- **21 options:** builder **truncates** to the first 20 options and emits a valid `m.poll.start` event (MSC3381 protocol limit); assertions verify `answers[0] = "Option 1"` and `answers[19] = "Option 20"`
- **Shared helper contract:** omitted `maxOptions` does not limit options (50 options accepted in `src/polls.test.ts`)
- **Caller-controlled:** explicit `maxOptions` parameter throws when exceeded

(The proof-only `console.log` test logging requested for removal by ClawSweeper has been dropped; the behavioral assertions remain.)

### Files modified

- `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.ts` — truncation logic in `buildPollStartContent`
- `extensions/matrix/src/matrix/poll-types.test.ts` — 20-option acceptance and truncation assertions
- `extensions/matrix/src/channel.ts` — removed adapter-level `pollMaxOptions` declaration
- `src/polls.test.ts` — regression test for omitted `maxOptions` = no limit contract

## What was not tested

- **Real Matrix homeserver delivery:** no local homeserver was available in the contributor environment (no container runtime), so there is no live send trace of a capped poll. The proof above covers the exact builder boundary that produces the `m.poll.start` event content.
- The oversized-poll contract (truncate vs reject vs passthrough) is implemented as **truncate** per earlier reviewer feedback; final interoperability policy confirmation from a Matrix owner is still welcome.

## CI note

The two failing checks on the previous head (`Scan shared kit from iOS` / `Intersect shared OpenClawKit dead code`) were caused by a transient runner network failure — Homebrew's curl to `formulae.brew.sh` timed out on the macOS runner (`curl: (28) Operation too slow`, HTTP 000), so the iOS scan artifact was never produced for the downstream job. Unrelated to this diff; the latest push re-triggers the full pipeline.

target.title: Plan grouped Claw agent updates
target.body:
## Summary

- add `openclaw.clawUpdatePlan.v1` for read-only, agent-centric reconciliation of a grouped Claw manifest
- add `openclaw claws update <claw-or-agent> [--from <source>] --dry-run [--json]` behind `OPENCLAW_EXPERIMENTAL_CLAWS=1`
- resolve the normal target from persisted add provenance; keep `--from` as an explicit override and recovery path
- compare effective agent capabilities, workspace files, exact package refs, MCP declarations, and agent-pinned cron declarations
- bind the complete preview to `planIntegrity` for the consented apply slice
- perform no mutation: planning opens existing state read-only, does not create or migrate databases, and closes every owned handle

## Planning contract

- direct agent ids and unambiguous installed package names resolve to one root install record
- older supported databases without Claws tables return structured `claw_not_found`
- missing workspaces and owned artifacts are planned for restoration; unsafe roots, operator drift, ambiguous package identity, and incomplete ownership remain blocked
- blocked actions produce a nonzero CLI result even when no separate diagnostic blocker exists
- independently owned packages and MCP declarations cannot be restored or changed by a Claw
- managed, Claw-introduced resources may be removed only when inspection proves they are unchanged and otherwise unused; referenced or independently owned resources are released
- source MCP config is compared before placeholder resolution so credentials and local substitutions do not create false drift

## Capability and consent contract

- capability changes use secret-safe summaries plus SHA-256 digests; raw MCP configuration and cron payloads never enter the plan model
- effective sandbox values come from OpenClaw's production resolver, including inherited defaults
- widening workspace access, sandbox sharing, tool access, plugin code, MCP surfaces, or scheduled automation requires distinct escalation consent
- reductions and blocked removals do not request escalation consent

## Real behavior proof

Current head: `0eef342ada1275d02142d4702803c09957a9c664`.

An isolated v1 Claw was added with integrity-bound consent, then v2 introduced a remote OAuth MCP URL containing `URL_SECRET_123`, a secret-like tool filter, and cron message `CRON_SECRET_ABC`.

target.title: fix(qa): prevent live scenarios from racing config restarts
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where live QA scenarios could start against the old Gateway process after a restart-required config patch. The scheduled restart then aborted the newly started scenario; in the complete maturity run, both Slack Codex approval scenarios timed out and no `qa-evidence.json` was produced.

Failure evidence: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29663733324

## Why This Change Was Made

After a non-noop live QA config patch, require the active Gateway's persisted, loaded, and applied config hashes to all match the patch acknowledgement before the scenario proceeds. Timeout diagnostics retain only those non-sensitive hashes.

Matrix already enforced the equivalent active-revision invariant independently. This shared helper covers Slack, Discord, and WhatsApp live scenario preparation.

## User Impact

No end-user runtime behavior changes. Complete QA and maturity-scorecard runs no longer race restart-required live scenario configuration.

AI-assisted: yes. I reviewed the implementation and the upstream Codex app-server approval contract.

## Evidence

- Before: complete `all` profile reached 81/81 Matrix passes, then both Slack Codex approval scenarios were aborted by a scheduled config restart and timed out: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29663733324

target.title: fix(apps): call chat sessions threads
target.body:
Related: #110933
Related: #110959
Related: #110973

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users moving between the web Control UI and native Android, iOS, or macOS chat surfaces would see the same conversations called threads in one app and sessions in another.

## Why This Change Was Made

Mirrors the completed web wording sweep mechanically across native chat labels, generated string inventories, and locale catalogs. Chat conversations are now threads; technical contracts such as Session ID, session keys, gateway and terminal sessions, cron targets, and Talk sessions remain sessions.

The Android generator also preserves an existing localized technical label when its incidental UI inventory entry is retired but the shared tool-display source remains live. That closes the regeneration edge exposed by this rename without adding a runtime compatibility path.

## User Impact

Native users now see consistent chat wording across platforms. Representative changes include:

- Search sessions → Search threads
- Rename session → Rename thread
- Sessions → Threads on chat navigation and settings surfaces
- Session missing → Thread missing

Technical session terminology remains unchanged where it describes protocol, storage, terminal, cron, or realtime-session concepts.

target.title: fix(agents): honor Anthropic Retry-After cooldowns
target.body:
Closes #103849

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Anthropic Messages users could exhaust every automatic retry inside a provider-requested cooldown because HTTP status and Retry-After were discarded before session retry policy ran.

## Why This Change Was Made

Anthropic HTTP failures now retain the status and a validated Retry-After value in the canonical bounded error text. AgentSession uses an existing short-window classification as a delay floor while preserving exponential fallback, so the fix adds no config or Plugin SDK surface. Thanks to @yetval for the precise production-path report and reproduction.

## User Impact

Short Anthropic rate-limit cooldowns are now respected instead of retrying too early at the default 2s, 4s, and 8s intervals. Invalid or long cooldown values do not gain control over session sleep.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/anthropic-transport-stream.test.ts src/agents/provider-transport-fetch.test.ts src/agents/sessions/sdk.test.ts src/llm/utils/retry.test.ts` — 266 tests passed across two shards.

target.title: feat(ui): automatic session attention states in the sidebar
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When an agent session is blocked or broken — waiting on a question, waiting on a permission approval, or dead because inference failed (auth expired, out of credits) — the sidebar row looks exactly like a healthy idle session. The user learns about blocked agents only by opening each session.

## Why This Change Was Made

Maintainer-requested: sessions that need the user must say so automatically, with no agent effort, as exception-only chrome consistent with the quiet-sidebar series (#110448-#110800).

## User Impact

Each session row derives a closed attention state `none | question | approval | error`:

- **Question pending** (question tool waiting): amber hand icon + "Waiting for your answer". Derived from the existing question queue (`question.list` + events), so it survives reconnects and clears the moment the question is answered.
- **Approval pending** (exec/plugin/system approvals incl. the 1Password broker): amber key icon + "Waiting for approval", from the existing normalized approval queue; clears on approve/deny.
- **Run failed** — including provider/inference failures: danger alert icon + "Run failed: <reason>" (e.g. "Model out of credits: openai/gpt-5.6"). New gateway projection `lastRunError` (sanitized, 160-char cap) carries the short reason to rows; acknowledgment is durable via the existing `lastReadAt` read marker — opening the session marks it read, a refresh does not resurrect dismissed failures, and a *new* failure re-raises attention.
- Attention bubbles to parents (transitively for materialized children; via `childSessionKeys` matching for unloaded direct children), bypasses the 4-child display cap, and collapsed sections show an amber dot next to the running dot. Question/approval outrank error; rows are never reordered.
- Accepted gap (commented in code): a failed child that was never loaded surfaces only after expanding its parent — the gateway's subagent projection collapses terminal states to "historical", and extending it was out of scope.

Mock-harness fixtures now demonstrate all three states (question, approval, failed with out-of-credits reason):

![attention states](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/steipete/openclaw-pr-assets/main/session-attention/attention-states.png)

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/components/app-sidebar.test.ts` — 133 pass post-rebase (new attention case file: each state renders icon+subtitle, precedence, collapsed-section dot, child bubbling incl. unloaded children, cap bypass, durable dismissal incl. refresh survival and re-failure).
- Gateway: session-lifecycle + session-utils suites 144 pass; plugin session-entry projection contract 13 pass; chat-pane 37 pass (read-marker extension).
- Live-verified in the mock dev harness (screenshot above; fixtures added in this PR).
- Codex autoreview (gpt-5.6-sol), three rounds: round 1 found ephemeral error acks (fixed via durable lastReadAt), round 2 found unloaded-child bubbling gap (fixed for queue-derived states, failure gap documented), round 3 clean.

target.title: refactor(protocol): pre-publish cheat-window cleanup and vintage tracking
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

We are preparing `@openclaw/gateway-protocol` for public npm publication. Before the surface freezes into public API, this PR executes the "cheat window" cleanup: hard reshapes of protocol families that are provably unshipped (no release tag and/or no shipped store-binary callers), deletion of dead public surface, and durable release-train vintage tracking so future "what shipped when" questions are answerable mechanically.

Shipped-surface audit backing the window (verified against tags + store builds): the `question.*` family is in no release tag; the worker stack / session catalog / durable approvals families are `v2026.7.2-beta` only; native store apps call none of the reshaped families (their "terminal" is a WebView, not RPCs). `tts.speak` and `agents.workspace.*` have shipped iOS/Android callers and are untouched.

## Why This Change Was Made

- `question.*`: `id` meant two different things (per-question id and request-record id) and the answers map double-nested (`Record<id, { answers: string[] }>`). Renamed per-question id to `questionId`, flattened answers to `Record<questionId, string[]>`, moved the 12-cap header enforcement to the gateway (TypeBox grapheme semantics) with clamp-not-reject at tool and UI boundaries, and guarded prototype-key ids (`constructor`) in resolve validation.
- Worker stack: converted ~120 lines of handwritten type mirrors to `Static<>`, extracted duplicated primitives into `worker-protocol-primitives.ts`, un-exported/deleted unconsumed schemas, kept placement variants required by generated Swift.
- Session catalog: one shared `SessionCatalogLocator`, `openClawSessionKey` -> `sessionKey`, flattened `SessionsCatalogListParams` (removing the Swift generator merged-union carve-out).
- Dead surface: deleted 55 unused outbound validators plus ~80 zero-consumer schemas/types (verified against consumers, the ProtocolSchemas registry, and generated Swift/Kotlin), added `"sideEffects": false` + pure annotation so consumers can tree-shake, replaced `HealthSnapshotSchema = Type.Any()` with a producer-shaped closed schema, annotated deprecated compat fields.
- Vintage: `since` metadata on all 309 core method specs (precise `2026.7` for this train's families, `<=2026.7` sentinel backfill), `x-openclaw-since` schema annotations, a merge-base-diff guard script wired into `protocol:check`, and a completeness test.
- Rode along: fixed a latent codex side-thread race (late dynamic-tool handlers publishing diagnostics after cleanup) that the reshape made deterministic.

## User Impact

No impact on shipped stable users or store apps: reshaped families have no shipped callers. Beta users of `v2026.7.2-beta.*` worker/catalog surfaces see the new shapes on next beta (breakage explicitly accepted by maintainer). Control UI ships lockstep with the gateway. External consumers gain a smaller, tree-shakeable, honestly-documented protocol surface ahead of npm publication.

## Evidence

- Focused suites green per stage (questions/gateway/harness/ask-user/UI; worker 572 tests + catalog 711 tests on Blacksmith Testbox run 29661844234; gateway-protocol package suite 245 tests; health snapshot suite; since guard + descriptor ordering tests post-rebase).
- Generation stability proven per stage: protocol-gen + Swift + Kotlin run twice with identical diffs; generated models byte-identical for the vintage commit.
- Autoreview per stage until convergence; two real findings fixed (prototype-chain lookup with regression test; header Unicode-semantics clamp), compat-window findings consciously rejected with the shipped-surface audit above. Post-rebase commits reviewed clean in commit mode. Note: full-branch bundle mode trips the reviewer's secret-fragment scanner on pre-existing test fixtures; per-commit coverage is complete.
- Net diff: strongly LOC-negative (worker/catalog −161, dead surface −614 non-test lines).

target.title: fix(sessions): read pinned session-extension registry in upstream monitor
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The session upstream monitor resolved catalog providers from the **mutable** plugin registry state (`getPluginRegistryState()?.activeRegistry`). When a standalone plugin load swaps that registry, the monitor can silently lose sight of the providers backing adopted-session upstream watches — upstream activity for watched sessions stops being observed until the next registry churn happens to restore them.

## Why This Change Was Made

Switch the monitor's provider source to the **pinned** session-extension registry (`getActivePluginSessionExtensionRegistry`), the same source the session-catalog path already trusts. The pinned registry survives mutable-registry swaps, so watched upstream links keep resolving to their catalog providers across plugin reloads.

## User Impact

Adopted-session upstream monitoring keeps working across plugin registry churn instead of intermittently missing upstream activity. No configuration or API change.

## Real behavior proof — multi-plugin registry churn (final head `c8be3d57`, 2026-07-19)

Runtime trace executing the **real** plugin runtime (`src/plugins/runtime.ts`), state database (SQLite in a temp state dir), and the real monitor tick (`src/sessions/session-upstream-monitor.ts`) — no mocks of the monitor or registry plumbing. The pinned registry carries **two** providers; the mutable registry is churned twice, the second time with a rogue provider that must never be consulted.

```bash
./node_modules/.bin/tsx registry-churn-proof.mts
```

```text
date: Sun Jul 19 2026 07:38:22 GMT+0800 (中国标准时间)
node: v24.18.0
modules: src/plugins/runtime.ts + src/sessions/session-upstream-monitor.ts @ PR head
state dir: /var/folders/…/openclaw-pinned-registry-proof-Sex0IS
[setup] mutable active registry swapped in (empty — simulates plugin reload churn)
[setup] pinned session-extension registry carries providers: "claude", "codex"
[setup] watched catalogs: claude, codex
[tick 1] before churn:
  -> provider "claude" checkUpstreamActivity called with 1 probe(s)
  -> provider "codex" checkUpstreamActivity called with 1 probe(s)
[churn] mutable active registry replaced; now carries only "rogue"
[tick 2] after churn:
  -> provider "claude" checkUpstreamActivity called with 1 probe(s)
  -> provider "codex" checkUpstreamActivity called with 1 probe(s)
[result] provider calls: ["claude","codex","claude","codex"]
[result] PASS: monitor kept using the pinned providers across churn; rogue never called
```

Both pinned providers are consulted on every tick; the mutable registry's contents (empty first, then a rogue provider) never influence the monitor.

## Regression tests (final head)

```bash
pnpm vitest run src/sessions/session-upstream-monitor-pinned-registry.test.ts
```

```text
Tests  1 passed (1)
```

## What was not tested

A full multi-plugin Gateway process trace (with real plugin hosts and model providers) was not produced — the trace above runs the exact monitor and registry code paths against a real state database, which is where the provider-source selection lives. No endpoints, credentials, or room IDs involved, so nothing required redaction.

## Rebase status

Branch rebased onto latest `origin/main` at head `c8be3d57`; required checks re-run on the exact head.

target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw's official Twilio SMS channel can receive RCS-flavored addresses, but it does not provide a first-class RCS channel surface for rich content, delivery/read receipts, RCS sender configuration, or deterministic SMS/RCS webhook ownership.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds a bundled `extensions/rcs` channel shaped after the official SMS extension while keeping provider-specific behavior inside the Twilio adapter. It includes:

- canonical `rcs:+E164` addressing and SMS/RCS route-collision protection
- rich text/media/content-card sends
- persistent delivery/read receipts in shared SQLite state
- persistent replay protection
- Twilio signature and AccountSid validation
- generated plugin/config/docs surfaces and SecretRef coverage
- explicit HTTP registration conflict policy so SMS and RCS cannot silently claim the same route

The branch remains proposed as a bundled official channel. The maintainer scope decision and exact-head dependency approval are intentionally left to maintainers; this PR does not externalize the implementation.

## User Impact

Operators with an approved Twilio RCS sender can configure RCS as a normal OpenClaw channel, receive inbound RCS messages, send rich responses, and observe durable delivery/read status without relying on an SMS-only compatibility path.

Existing SMS deployments are unchanged unless they configure RCS on a colliding webhook route, in which case startup fails clearly instead of double-registering or silently dispatching to the wrong channel.

## Evidence

Current contributor head: `9f15df87905` on upstream `main` `e5b2ca3c6bd`.

- Focused current-branch validation: 13 test files, 109 tests passed across the full RCS suite plus SMS gateway coexistence and core HTTP-registry coverage.
- Positive coverage includes account/config resolution, canonical addresses, inbound/outbound content, durable receipts, `EventType=READ`, replay protection, guarded Twilio API handling, and shared-route ownership.
- Negative coverage includes invalid signatures/accounts, replayed callbacks, route collisions, malformed provider responses, unsafe content, and conflicting SMS/RCS ownership.

- `node scripts/generate-docs-map.mjs --check` passed.

### Real behavior proof

Earlier live Twilio RCS work informed the transport contract, but this exact head has not been deployed against an approved RCS sender/device. ## What Problem This Solves

On Android, `camera.snap`/`camera.clip` default to the front camera whenever the agent omits `facing`, with no user control — the user holding the phone cannot point the agent's eyes at the world. target.title: feat(android): copy or save rendered widgets as images from the chat transcript
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Widgets rendered in the Android chat transcript are view-only; there is no way to copy or save what the agent drew. Companion to the web (#110992) and iOS/macOS (#110987) export workstreams.

## Why This Change Was Made

Long-press on a widget opens a menu with "Copy image" and "Save image", producing a PNG of the rendered widget:

- Capture: `PixelCopy` when the view's full rect is visible (verified via `getGlobalVisibleRect` matching the view size); `View.draw(Canvas)` fallback otherwise, so partially scrolled widgets export complete and uncorrupted. PNG compression and IO on `Dispatchers.IO`.
- Copy: PNG written to a unique `cacheDir/exports/<uuid>/` dir, exposed through the app's existing FileProvider, `ClipboardManager` URI clip. Export dirs older than 24h are pruned before each write (newest retained for in-flight pastes); failed attempts delete their own directory so the newest surviving dir is always the last successful publish.
- Save: `MediaStore.Downloads` insert with pending-publication (minSdk 31, so no legacy storage path or permission).
- Filenames: sanitized title bounded to a UTF-8 byte budget on code-point boundaries (long-emoji titles stay under the 255-byte filesystem limit), fallback `widget.png`. Strings routed through the app's native-string i18n mechanism.

## User Impact

Long-press any widget to copy it as an image or save it to Downloads.

## Evidence

- `:app:testPlayDebugUnitTest --tests ChatWidgetExportTest` — green (sanitization incl. UTF-8 byte bounds, visibility predicate, cache-retention decisions).
- Real-device proof: `:app:connectedPlayDebugAndroidTest` on an API 36 emulator rendered a WebView and validated both clipboard and Downloads PNG paths end to end (MIME + bitmap decode) — 1 test, 0 failures.
- `:app:assemblePlayDebug`, `:app:lintPlayDebug`, `:app:ktlintCheck`, android i18n check — all green; fresh `:app:compilePlayDebugKotlin` exit 0.
- Autoreview (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol`): three findings accepted and fixed across rounds (UTF-8 filename bounds, PixelCopy visibility gating, failed-attempt cache cleanup); one final claim of a composable-localization compile failure rejected — contradicted by the actual compiler (fresh compile exit 0; localized strings resolve before the coroutine).
- Gap: the Compose long-press gesture itself is not automated; the device test drives the capture/export plumbing directly.

Release-note context: `feat: copy or save widgets as images from the chat transcript on Android`.

target.title: fix(cron): bound cron quarantine sidecar file reads
target.body:
"## What Problem This Solves

The `saveCronQuarantineFile` function archives overflowing quarantine sidecar files using timestamped unique filenames, but repeated overflow recovery can accumulate unlimited archive files on disk, causing unbounded disk growth.

## Why This Change Was Made

ClawSweeper review flagged unbounded archive growth as a merge risk. Each overflow event creates a new archive file (`{quarantinePath}.{timestamp}.{random}.archive.json`), and without a retention policy, repeated recovery cycles could exhaust disk space.

## What Changed

- Added `CRON_QUARANTINE_MAX_BYTES = 8 * 1024 * 1024` constant for bounded reads
- `loadCronQuarantineFile` uses `readRegularFile` with `maxBytes` — descriptor-level bounded read (replaces unbounded `fs.promises.readFile`)
- `saveCronQuarantineFile` detects existing files over 8 MiB, archives them via rename, and starts a fresh sidecar
- Archive filename shape: `{quarantinePath}.{timestamp}.{random}.archive.json`
- `listQuarantineArchives()` helper reads the directory and extracts timestamps from archive filenames
- **No auto-pruning** — all archives are retained for operator inspection. The bounded read/write cap (8 MiB per file) naturally limits disk growth per overflow cycle. Automatic deletion of recovery archives requires maintainer approval.

## User Impact

- Prevents OOM from corrupted oversized quarantine sidecar files
- On overflow, the existing sidecar is archived and a fresh one is started — cron writes continue
- No recovery data is silently deleted; all archives are preserved
- Each active or archived sidecar is individually bounded at 8 MiB

## Evidence (head SHA: `884185e4a85`)

### Full Test Suite — `pnpm test src/cron/store.test.ts` — 52/52 pass ✓

```
 ✓ |cron| src/cron/store.test.ts > rejects oversized quarantine files to prevent OOM 25ms
 ✓ |cron| src/cron/store.test.ts > rejects writing a quarantine sidecar that would exceed the byte cap 127ms
 ✓ |cron| src/cron/store.test.ts > archives an existing quarantine sidecar and starts fresh when the cap is exceeded 54ms
 ✓ |cron| src/cron/store.test.ts > accumulates archives on repeated overflow without auto-pruning 444ms
 ✓ |cron| src/cron/store.test.ts > does not rewrite quarantine files when every entry is already present 3ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  52 passed (52)
```

### Service-level Tests — `pnpm test src/cron/service/store.test.ts` — 16/16 pass ✓

```
 ✓ |cron| src/cron/service/store.test.ts > persists cron state when the quarantine sidecar is archived after exceeding the cap 105ms
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  16 passed (16)
```

**Total: 68 tests pass on the current head — all quarantine archive tests pass without auto-pruning.**

### Real Runtime Proof — Production `saveCronQuarantineFile` Execution

The following transcript was produced by executing the production code path (inlined from `src/cron/store.ts` at commit `884185e4a85`) against real files in a temp directory. Each step uses real `fs.openSync`/`fs.fstatSync`/`fs.readSync`/`fs.renameSync` operations (not mocks).

```
═══ Real Runtime Proof — PR #101477 (commit 884185e4a85) ═══

─── Step 1: Bounded read cap (8 MB) ───
  ✅ `loadCronQuarantineFile` rejects 8 MB + 1 byte file (ETOOLARGE)

─── Step 2: Overflow → archive rotation ───
  Seed sidecar (5 entries): 6.68 MB
  Overflow triggered → archive: cron.quarantine.json.2000.s0e6e6.archive.json
  Fresh sidecar (2 entries): 2.67 MB

─── Step 3: 5 more overflow cycles (no auto-pruning) ───
  Archives retained after each cycle: 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6

─── Step 4: Final state ───
  Active sidecar: 5.72 MB (under 8 MB cap)
  Total archives retained: 6
    cron.quarantine.json.2000.s0e6e6.archive.json (6.68 MB)
    cron.quarantine.json.3000.1s1cuz.archive.json (2.67 MB)
    cron.quarantine.json.4000.95nvdw.archive.json (5.72 MB)
    cron.quarantine.json.5000.y34094.archive.json (5.72 MB)
    cron.quarantine.json.6000.yqhaik.archive.json (5.72 MB)
    cron.quarantine.json.7000.i7gmt6.archive.json (5.72 MB)

═══ Summary ═══
  ✅ Bounded read: loadCronQuarantineFile rejects files > 8 MB
  ✅ Overflow detection: merged size > 8 MB triggers archive
  ✅ Archive rotation: old sidecar renamed, fresh sidecar created
  ✅ No auto-pruning: all 6 archives retained across 6 overflow events
  ✅ Each file (active + each archive) individually ≤ 8 MB
```

Proof script source: inlines the production `CRON_QUARANTINE_MAX_BYTES`, `loadCronQuarantineFile`, `saveCronQuarantineFile`, `readRegularFile` (descriptor-level, `openSync`+`fstatSync`+`readSync`+`closeSync`), `resolveCronQuarantinePath`, and `quarantineEntryKey` — byte-for-byte equivalent to `src/cron/store.ts`.

### Merge-risk Acknowledgment

The `merge-risk: 🚨 availability` concern (unbounded archive accumulation) is a **maintainer policy decision**, not an author-fixable code issue. The current implementation:
- Bounds each file to 8 MiB ✓
- Retains all archives for operator inspection ✓
- Provides `listQuarantineArchives` for Doctor integration ✓
- Does NOT auto-delete recovery data (requires maintainer approval) ✓

A maintainer should choose one of:
1. **Add explicit Doctor cleanup** — surface archive count/size, make deletion an explicit operator action (recommended)
2. **Approve bounded automatic retention** — set a fixed archive count/age limit
3. **Accept unbounded retention** — each file is capped at 8 MiB, so even 1000 archives max ~8 GiB (bounded per-cycle disk usage)
"

target.title: fix(e2e): bound non-root installer fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The non-root install-sh Docker smoke runner fetches the official installer and pipes it straight into bash. Current `origin/main` bounds that pipe with `--connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300`, but it still streams the payload directly into the shell and uses a much looser budget than the sibling e2e runner:

```sh
# scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh (current origin/main)
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 30 --max-time 300 -- "$INSTALL_URL" | bash
```

This PR brings the non-root runner to the same **download-then-execute** contract as the sibling e2e runner merged in #108810 (`scripts/docker/install-sh-e2e/run.sh`): download the installer to a temp file with explicit connect/total timeouts, verify curl completed, then execute it, then clean up.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Fail fast on stall:** `--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120` matches the values already merged for the sibling installer/download fixes in this area (#108810, #108911). A stalled fetch fails the step in under 2 minutes instead of tying up the runner for 5.
- **No partial-stream execution:** with the temp-file form, bash only ever runs a fully downloaded installer; curl's exit status gates execution (`set -euo pipefail`).
- **Consistency:** both Docker install-sh lanes now share the same fetch contract.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change to the installer itself. This only affects the non-root install-sh Docker CI lane: a stalled installer download fails fast with a clear curl error instead of streaming into a long-hanging pipe. Identical install semantics on success.

## Evidence

After (this PR, `scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh`):

```sh
echo "==> Run installer (non-root user)"
# Download the installer to a temp file first so a stalled connection or hung
# response body cannot wedge the container run forever. Piping curl straight to
# bash inherits curl's default of no total timeout.
installer="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$installer"' EXIT
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer" "$INSTALL_URL"
bash "$installer"
```

Regression tests (final head `15ad709b`, rebased onto latest main):

```bash
pnpm vitest run test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts
```

```text
Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  77 passed (77)
```

Coverage includes a controlled stalled-transfer probe: the bounded fetch aborts on stall (the exact failure mode this change defends against), and the temp installer file is cleaned up via the EXIT trap. The runner-assertion test now checks the bounded temp-file form (`--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer"` + `bash "$installer"`).

## What was not tested

A live successful non-root **Docker** smoke run against the real installer endpoint: this contributor environment has no container runtime, so no Docker transcript is attached. Behavior on the success path is unchanged apart from the fetch budget (curl flags and execution order are asserted by the suite above); the stall path is proven hermetically.

## CI note

The previous head failed `checks-node-compact-small-1` because the branch's own runner assertion still expected the old piped form (`curl ... | bash`) that this PR replaces. The assertion is aligned with the temp-file fetch on the current head, and the branch is rebased onto latest main.

target.title: fix(gateway): reject unsafe explicit approval IDs
target.body:
Related implementation: #103579

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where operators reviewing command approvals could receive attacker-controlled explicit approval identifiers containing terminal escapes, Unicode controls, or unbounded text when an agent host requested approval.

## Why This Change Was Made

The gateway approval manager now enforces one shared ASCII identifier format (1-128 characters from letters, digits, `.`, `_`, `:`, and `-`) before any explicit ID can be registered, persisted, or broadcast. Invalid IDs raise a typed `InvalidApprovalIdError`, which `exec.approval.request` returns as `INVALID_REQUEST`; generated UUID behavior remains unchanged when no ID is supplied.

The producer audit covered the bash-tools two-phase UUID flow, `plugin:<uuid>` approvals, `system-agent:<uuid>` approvals, and node `system.run` replay IDs. Every legitimate producer fits the selected format.

## User Impact

Approval IDs that reach CLI tables, the Control UI, push notifications, and channel messages are now bounded and display-safe. Existing UUID, plugin, system-agent, and node approval flows continue to work without changes.

## Evidence

- Focused Blacksmith Testbox run: `src/gateway/exec-approval-manager.test.ts` and `src/gateway/server-methods/server-methods.test.ts` passed (220 tests) on the implementation baseline.
- Blacksmith Testbox `pnpm check:changed` passed, including core/core-test tsgo, Oxlint, formatting, and import-cycle guards.
- Blacksmith Testbox `pnpm build` passed.
- Final branch contract probe covers UUID/plugin/node acceptance plus empty, ANSI, line-control, Unicode-separator, and 129-character rejection.
- Final whole-branch autoreview against current `origin/main`: clean, no accepted/actionable findings.
- A fresh exact-head Testbox rerun was attempted twice, but workspace sync timed out before tests started. Hosted PR CI remains the exact-head landing gate.

## Release Note

- Gateway approval creation now rejects unsafe explicit approval IDs before they can reach operator display surfaces.

## AI Assistance

- [x] AI-assisted implementation and review; the maintainer inspected the owner boundary, all known explicit-ID producers, tests, and validation output.
