**Observed result after fix:**
- Stalled `putNostrProfile` aborts after exactly **15,016ms** (within the 15s bound) and raises `AbortError`
- Stalled `importNostrProfile` aborts after exactly **15,006ms** (within the 15s bound) and raises `AbortError`
- Normal `putNostrProfile` requests complete in **15ms** (fast, no timeout)
- Normal `importNostrProfile` requests complete in **4ms** (fast, no timeout)
- All timeout tests pass with real wall-clock time, proving the abort mechanism works correctly
- Error type is correctly `AbortError` with message "This operation was aborted"

**What was tested:**
- Real wall-clock timeout behavior (not fake timers) against a deliberately stalled local HTTP server
- Normal operation round trips complete in milliseconds
- AbortError is correctly raised and can be caught/handled by UI code
- Timeout mechanism works for both publish and import operations
- Both quick-regression tests (fake timers) and real-behavior tests (real timers) pass
- The real-timeout suite saves the original `globalThis.fetch` before installing its relative-URL bridge and restores it in `afterEach`, so no bridge leaks into later tests; both Nostr suites were rerun after this teardown repair (results above)
- The repo-wide type-suppression inventory passes (`as-any` count stays at 0); the fetch bridge assigns `globalThis.fetch` through the standard typed signature
- No persistent data-model change: the diff only touches the two Nostr profile helpers and their test files; nothing is serialized, stored, or migrated

**Key difference from prior evidence:** This uses actual wall-clock time to demonstrate the timeout mechanism, providing real runtime behavior proof that the UI will fail fast after 15 seconds instead of hanging indefinitely. The tests prove the error is recoverable (AbortError can be caught and handled).

target.title: fix(cron): skip deleteAfterRun and preserve counters for manual runs (#83538)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`openclaw cron run` (a manual/operator run) on a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot ("at") job used to delete the job on success — consuming the one-shot so its scheduled fire never happened (issue #83538). Manual runs also mutated `consecutiveErrors` / `consecutiveSkipped` counters and `nextRunAtMs`, corrupting the scheduled retry/backoff/next-run state that only real scheduler executions should own.

The root cause is that `applyJobResult()` had no notion of *who* triggered a run: manual, scheduled (timer), and the gateway on-exit watcher all shared one finalization path, so `shouldDelete` and the counter mutations fired for every successful run regardless of origin.

## Why This Change Was Made

The fix threads an explicit `CronRunOrigin` (`"timer" | "watcher-terminal" | "operator"`) through cron finalization. `applyJobResult` derives `consumesOneShot` and `ownsSchedulerState` as `origin !== "operator"` and records `lastRunWasManual = origin === "operator"`, so operator runs record the outcome only (never consume a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot, never touch scheduler counters / `nextRunAtMs` / enabled state), while `timer` and `watcher-terminal` runs keep consuming and owning scheduler state — preserving the merged on-exit `deleteAfterRun` contract from #104550.

`origin` is kept strictly internal. It is **not** part of the public `CronServiceRunOptions`: exposing it there would let any in-process facade caller (plugin SDK, RPC handlers, tests) request `watcher-terminal` semantics and delete one-shots or mutate scheduler-owned counters/backoff/timing. Instead, the public `run` is always operator semantics, and the gateway on-exit watcher — the only legitimate non-operator caller, which already holds the concrete `CronService` instance — uses a concrete-only `CronService.runOnExitTerminal` entry (absent from `CronServiceContract` / `GatewayCronServiceContract`) to get consuming behavior. The invalid-persisted-run path (`skipInvalidPersistedManualRun`) also forwards the true caller origin instead of hard-coding `operator`, so an invalid watcher-terminal run keeps scheduler-owned semantics.

## User Impact

- Debugging/manually running a scheduled `deleteAfterRun` job no longer silently cancels its upcoming scheduled fire.
- Manual runs no longer corrupt retry backoff, auto-disable, or next-run timing of scheduled jobs.
- Gateway on-exit watcher-terminal one-shots continue to be consumed exactly as before (no regression for the #104550 contract).
- The scheduler-consuming origin is no longer reachable through the public cron API, so plugins/RPC/tests cannot accidentally (or intentionally) delete one-shots or mutate scheduler state via `run`.

## Evidence

Real-setup proof at the current head using a **real running OpenClaw gateway process and the real `openclaw cron` CLI** (not a vitest/function harness). Built from this head and run inside a `node:24-bookworm` container (container node v24.18.0; the repo engines floor is 24.15.0), against a real on-disk cron store (sqlite).

```
Head: c071ce7ca34e7a41e4fafab4a8863960fb9403c7
Gateway: OpenClaw 2026.7.2 (c071ce7)   dist/build-info.json commit = c071ce7c...

Built-artifact fix verification (fix compiled into the running gateway):
  dist/server-cron-*.js contains:
    async runOnExitTerminal(id, payload) { ... }
    run: (jobId, payload) => cron.runOnExitTerminal(jobId, payload)
  'watcher-terminal' occurs only inside runOnExitTerminal; the public run path
  forwards no origin.

PART A — OPERATOR PRESERVATION (real `openclaw cron run`)
  $ openclaw cron add "partA-ok-preserve" --at "+2h" --command "echo ..." --delete-after-run
    -> id 3c309f88..., nextRunAtMs 1784045230759
  $ openclaw cron run 3c309f88... --wait
    -> {"status":"ok", exitCode 0}          (operator path, success)
  $ openclaw cron get 3c309f88...
    -> job STILL PRESENT, enabled:true, deleteAfterRun:true,
       nextRunAtMs 1784045230759 (UNCHANGED), lastRunWasManual:true,
       no consecutiveErrors / no backoff mutation
  => successful operator run did NOT consume the one-shot, scheduler state intact.

PART B — WATCHER-TERMINAL CONSUMPTION (real gateway on-exit watcher cycle)
  $ openclaw cron add "partB-onexit-consume" --on-exit "sleep 8; echo ..." \
        --command "echo ..." --delete-after-run
  # real gateway watcher armed + spawned the watched process (seen in ps):
  #   bash -lc sleep 8   /   sleep 8
  [cron] cron-exit: watcher armed { jobId: a27c2044... }
  [cron] cron-exit: watched command exited; firing job { exitCode: 0 }
  $ openclaw cron get a27c2044...      -> "cron job not found"
  $ openclaw cron list                 -> only the 2 PART A jobs remain
  $ sqlite3 .../openclaw.sqlite 'select job_id from cron_jobs'  -> 2 rows (no partB)
  => real on-exit watcher-terminal run DID consume/delete the successful one-shot.

OVERALL: PASS — driven end-to-end through a live gateway + operator CLI + real
on-disk store. Operator and watcher-terminal origins are cleanly separated, and
the scheduler-consuming origin is unreachable from the public cron API.
```

Unit/regression coverage at head: the public `CronServiceContract.run` preserves a `deleteAfterRun` one-shot (operator semantics, no scheduler-state mutation) even though it can no longer request another origin, `CronService.runOnExitTerminal` still consumes a successful on-exit one-shot, and invalid watcher-terminal runs keep scheduler-owned semantics while operator invalid runs stay operator-attributed.

Persisted-state coverage for `lastRunWasManual` (`timer.backoff-config-readback.test.ts`, real on-disk sqlite store): a **fresh store** where a manual/operator error run persists `lastRunWasManual: true`, reloads from sqlite, and keeps the natural next-run slot (no backoff floor, `consecutiveErrors` untouched) so the scheduled fire still triggers on a fresh service state; and an **upgraded store** whose persisted job predates the field (no `lastRunWasManual` on disk) — on reload the absent field is treated as a scheduled run, so the error backoff window still applies and the past-due slot is correctly suppressed. This proves the new optional field degrades safely for both new and pre-existing stores.

### Proof equivalence: transcript head → current head

The live-setup transcript above was captured at `c071ce7c`. The branch head has since been rebased onto newer `main` (current head `c42041b0`). Scoped to the cron runtime surface exercised by the transcript (`src/cron/service/`, `src/gateway/server-cron.ts`), the full non-test delta between `c071ce7c` and the current head is:

- **`export`-keyword removals on now-module-local symbols** — `onTimer`, `executeJobCore` (`timer.ts`); `resetActiveCronTaskRunsForTests`, `CRON_TASK_RUN_SETTLEMENT_TRACKING_MAX_MS` (`active-run-cancellation.ts`); `DEFAULT_JOB_TIMEOUT_MS`, `AGENT_TURN_SAFETY_TIMEOUT_MS` (`timeout-policy.ts`). Values and in-module usage unchanged; no prod file outside each defining module imported them.
- **test-support extraction** — `timer.ts` and `active-run-cancellation.ts` now expose those test-only helpers via a `globalThis` symbol registered inside an `if (process.env.VITEST || process.env.NODE_ENV === "test")` guard, imported by new `*.test-support.ts` modules. This block is a no-op in a production gateway.
- **four appended `/* oxlint-disable max-lines */` directive comments** (`jobs.ts`, `ops.ts`, `timer.ts`, `server-cron.ts`).
- **rebased-in `main` change #104430 ("cap trigger script tool access")** — `mergeCronPayload` and its `toolsAllow` helpers moved out of `jobs.ts` into the new `src/cron/service/payload-merge.ts`, with cross-payload-kind `toolsAllow` marker handling. This is genuine upstream behavior on the `cron.update` payload-merge / trigger-script tool-access surface, disjoint from scheduler counters and one-shot consumption; it arrived through the rebase and is not part of this PR's proof scope.
- **`server-cron.ts` `toolsAllow` type-guard simplification** — the trigger-script call now reads `job.payload.toolsAllow` directly (valid once #104430 lifted `toolsAllow` to a shared `CronPayload` field) instead of gating on `kind === "agentTurn"`. This is on the trigger-script tool-access path, not the `runOnExitTerminal` / delete-after-run wiring.

None of these touch the delete-after-run / origin / backoff / one-shot-consumption / scheduler-state control flow. The `CronRunOrigin` threading, `consumesOneShot` / `ownsSchedulerState` (`origin !== "operator"`), `lastRunWasManual` (`origin === "operator"`), `shouldDelete = wouldDelete && consumesOneShot` in `timer.ts`, the `ops.ts` origin forwarding, and the `runOnExitTerminal` wiring in `server-cron.ts` are unchanged. The recorded operator-preservation and watcher-terminal-consumption behavior therefore holds on the current head. Reviewers can confirm the delta with:

```
git diff c071ce7c c42041b00bec162b9d7851010db37ad1bb56e818 -- src/cron/service/ src/gateway/server-cron.ts
```


### Follow-up fix: manual ok run must not strand the one-shot slot

A further defect on the same origin-threading surface: a **due** `deleteAfterRun` one-shot `at` job that receives an **operator (manual) ok run** keeps its `nextRunAtMs` preserved (operator runs do not consume the one-shot), but `computeJobNextRunAtMs`'s `at`-branch collapsed the pending slot to `undefined` whenever the last run status was `ok`. The next expired-slot maintenance recompute then wiped the slot, stranding the job as a zombie that never fires and never deletes. Existing coverage only exercised `skipped` runs, so the `ok` path was missed.

Fix: the ok-branch collapse in `computeJobNextRunAtMs` is now guarded by `lastRunWasManual !== true`, so only a scheduler-owned (timer) ok run retires the slot; manual/operator ok runs leave the pending scheduled fire intact. This reuses the already-persisted `lastRunWasManual` field, so it is restart-safe with no new state or migration (an absent field on a pre-upgrade store is treated as a scheduled run, preserving prior behavior). A regression test drives a manual ok run on a due deleteAfterRun one-shot through the maintenance recompute and a restart reload (slot preserved both times), then a real scheduled timer tick that fires and deletes it.

target.title: fix: distinct Responses tool-call ids for repeated native Kimi calls
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Resolves a problem where users on the `openai-responses` API path would stop getting any agent replies at all once a session called the same tool at the same call-index more than once (a common pattern — e.g. a `gateway`/status-check tool invoked first in several separate turns). Every subsequent turn on that session failed before producing a reply, with the gateway logging `invalid_replay_transcript: ... dangling_tool_call toolCallId=call_<hash>`. The session was effectively bricked until manually truncated or reset.

Observed on `moonshotai/kimi-k2.5` via OpenRouter, which is what my agent was routed to at the time. The bug isn't model-specific, though — it's in OpenClaw's own id normalizer for the `openai-responses` wire format, so it reproduces for any model/provider combination that goes through that API shape and reuses native `functions.<tool>:<index>|fc_*`-style ids across turns.

## Why This Change Was Made

`normalizeOpenAIResponsesFunctionCallId` (`src/agents/embedded-agent-helpers/openai.ts`) rewrites native tool-call ids like `functions.gateway:0|fc_tmp_kegospxl46` into `call_*` ids the OpenAI Responses API accepts. It splits the id into a `callId` half (`functions.gateway:0`) and an `itemId` half (`fc_tmp_kegospxl46`), but only hashed the `callId` half when generating the `call_*` id. Since `callId` is just `<toolName>:<callIndexInTurn>`, it repeats across turns whenever the same tool is called at the same position — so every occurrence collapsed to the identical `call_*` id, corrupting replay once two or more calls collided in the same session history.

The fix hashes the full `callId|itemId` pairing (falling back to `callId` alone when there is no `itemId`), so repeated native ids that share a `callId` now normalize to distinct ids while still resolving consistently between the assistant tool-call and its matching tool-result.

## User Impact

Sessions on `openai-responses`-backed providers no longer get permanently stuck after the same tool is called at the same index more than once in a conversation — replies keep working instead of failing on every turn with a replay error.

## Evidence

- [x] Mark as AI-assisted in the PR title or description — root-caused and fixed with an AI coding assistant (Claude Code) after diagnosing the issue on a personal OpenClaw instance; I reviewed and understand the change.

**Full before/after runtime proof (linked artifact):** https://gist.github.com/christiandesantis/b1cee60d56319d2d80013310a0ba9cb8 — verbatim `openclaw logs`/`openclaw sessions list --json`/`openclaw agent --json` output from my own instance: session `agent:main:main` (`980f8d6e-c602-4540-b54d-20602bab3d0f`) status `"failed"` before the patch with the repeated `dangling_tool_call` error, then `"done"` after, plus the `workspace.test.ts` CI-flake repro from below. Nothing in it is sensitive — just error metadata, session/run ids, and JSON structure, no personal data.

**Root cause repro** (standalone, no runtime needed):
```
$ node -e 'console.log(require("crypto").createHash("sha256").update("functions.gateway:0").digest("hex").slice(0,10))'
24933ffc9b
```
This matches the exact `toolCallId` from the failure below — proving the collision is `sha256("functions.gateway:0")`, i.e. the `callId` half alone, independent of which specific call produced it.

**Before fix** — real gateway log from my own OpenClaw instance, `agent:main:main` session, every single turn failing identically:
```

2026-07-18T14:46:46.695-04:00 error diagnostic lane task error: lane=main durationMs=253 error="Error: invalid_replay_transcript: OpenAI Responses replay contains dangling_tool_call toolCallId=call_functions_gateway_0_24933ffc9b at message index 18"
```

target.title: fix: cloud-worker results are lost when the box dies before reconciliation
target.body:
Related: #110224 (phase 1 of 3)

## What Problem This Solves

Resolves the data-loss half of #110224: a cloud-worker turn's file result only existed on the leased box until a clean workspace apply succeeded. If inbound reconciliation failed (real local divergence) and the box then died — or the Gateway restarted and its recovery sweep found the environment gone — the unaccepted result was abandoned and the placement force-failed, permanently losing the turn's work. Observed live during a cloud-workers stress test (full incident log in #110224).

## Why This Change Was Made

Stage-first reconciliation: when a worker result is pulled, the complete result tree is committed as a durable Git ref in the session workspace repo (`refs/openclaw/worker-results/<claim>`, with a crash-safe candidate ref during construction) before any apply is attempted, and recorded on the pending-result fence row (new nullable `staged_result_ref` column, state schema v5, additive migration). Apply and every retry then run from the staged tree as a purely local operation; the recovery sweep skips the tunnel entirely when a staged ref exists. Recovery semantics change accordingly: an unaccepted fence with a staged ref must never be destroyed by environment lifecycle — the environment can be reclaimed while the fence and placement stay alive until the local apply is durably accepted. Only legacy fences without a staged ref keep the old abandon path. Staged refs are deleted on acceptance or explicit abandonment; ref construction validates claim ids (`[A-Za-z0-9-]+`) and fails closed; ordering is candidate apply → quiescence/fence checks → canonical ref publish → SQLite pointer, so a crash at any step leaves a recoverable state. Object retention after ref deletion matches the existing managed-worktree snapshot pattern (`refs/openclaw/snapshots/*`).

Non-goals (later phases per #110224): conflict resolution policy, turn-claim release semantics, chat error copy, UI affordances.

Maintainer rulings for this PR: keep the state schema at `main + 1` (v5); the rollback consequence is deliberately accepted. Complete-tree staging and object-store retention parity with managed-worktree snapshots are also accepted design decisions.

## User Impact

A dead or reclaimed cloud box can no longer lose a finished turn's file changes: the result is already safe on the Gateway and is applied or retried locally. Gateway restarts preserve pending results instead of force-failing their placements.

## Evidence

- Focused tests: `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/worker-environments/ src/state/openclaw-state-db.test.ts` — 447 tests green (89 + 358 across shards), including: staging order (ref before apply), crash-gap adoption of canonical refs, dead-environment recovery applying from the staged ref without a tunnel, divergence keeping fence + placement alive, ref cleanup on accept, hostile git-hook neutralization, and the v4→v5 migration.
- Remote `pnpm check:changed` (Blacksmith Testbox): exit 0 (typecheck, lint, format, policy guards, import cycles).
- Structured autoreview (codex, gpt-5.6-sol): accepted findings fixed (ref-name validation, staging/finalization race reordering, candidate-ref leak); final run clean. Two rejected-by-owner suggestions documented inline (object-store retention parity with worktree snapshots; complete-tree vs delta storage is the requested contract).

### Real recovery proof

Exact head `a9d37cdda82c3bb1ce5092c9609a609366f31245` was built and run through an isolated real Gateway → bundled Crabbox provider → AWS worker path. The model side used the deterministic local QA provider; provisioning, bundle install, SSH/tunnel, worker runtime, workspace transfer, durable staging, lease loss, Gateway restart, and recovery were production paths.

The proof injected one persistence-boundary failure with an isolated SQLite trigger: reject the first `workspace_accepted_at_ms` update after the canonical staged Git ref was published. This models the crash window without modifying production code. It then stopped the actual AWS lease before restarting the Gateway.

```text
provider: aws
lease: cbx_f8b8fd6f4912 (stopped before Gateway restart; cleaned up)
pending before restart: staged_result_ref present, workspace_accepted_at_ms null
worker result before restart sha256: e0b584a31c3f16c59b04d9e00d0c4421618f0ad633ededdefa3e052fc401eb2c
worker result after restart sha256:  e0b584a31c3f16c59b04d9e00d0c4421618f0ad633ededdefa3e052fc401eb2c
pending rows after restart: 0
placement after restart: reclaimed
turn claim after restart: null
recovery_error after restart: null
staged Git ref after restart: absent
```

The first harness attempt reached an attached AWS worker but selected an empty side-database path before starting a turn; it failed during trigger installation and cleaned up its lease. The corrected run above used the Gateway's canonical `state/openclaw.sqlite` path and completed end to end.

target.title: chore(ui): add mock chat fixtures for design QA
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The Control UI mock has limited curated chat state for design QA, so reviewers have to rely on ad hoc sessions when checking empty chat, longer transcripts, markdown rendering, code blocks, tables, warnings, and recoverable error copy.

## Why This Change Was Made

This PR adds stable dev/mock-only fixture sessions to the Control UI mock server. The proposed fixtures cover a New session empty state, a coding session, a response-shape showcase, and a markdown showcase without changing production gateway or session APIs.

## User Impact

There is no production user-facing behavior change. Developers and designers can load stable mock chat sessions for future Control UI visual review.

## Evidence

- `git diff --check`
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check --threads=1 scripts/control-ui-mock-dev.ts`
- `pnpm dev:ui:mock -- --host 127.0.0.1 --port 5197`
- Browser smoke loaded these proposed mock routes and confirmed the expected fixture content:
  - `/chat?session=agent%3Aopenclaw-mock%3Anew-session`
  - `/chat?session=agent%3Aopenclaw-mock%3Aqa-coding-session`
  - `/chat?session=agent%3Aopenclaw-mock%3Aresponse-shape-showcase`
  - `/chat?session=agent%3Aopenclaw-mock%3Amarkdown-showcase`

target.body:
## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `test/filtered-bundle-mcp`, commit `d5bffb3dc0`, with an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: Created a temporary Codex-compatible bundle containing `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, `.mcp.json`, `skills/`, and `apps/`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins install --link <temp>/vision-mcp`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins inspect vision-mcp --json`; then loaded bundle MCP config with `node --import tsx` calling `loadEnabledBundleMcpConfig(...)` against the isolated home/config.

Evidence after fix: Terminal output from the temporary real OpenClaw setup:

```text

$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins install --link /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Linked plugin path: /var/folders/.../openclaw-bundle-proof.gE7Fjt/vision-mcp
Restart the gateway to load plugins.
$ node scripts/run-node.mjs plugins inspect vision-mcp --json
{
  "diagnostics": [],
  "command": "npx",
  "args": [
    "-y",
    "@vision-mcp/cli@latest",
```

## Summary

In this PR, the Appearance text-size setting applies across Control UI content typography instead of only affecting the chat transcript. target.title: fix(ci): skip Periphery scans for unrelated PR changes
target.body:
Related: #106090
Observed on: #106789

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where pull requests unrelated to iOS, macOS, or shared OpenClawKit could run Periphery scans when `main` advanced after the pull-request event was created. The stale event base SHA made base-branch changes look like pull-request changes, consuming macOS runners and adding irrelevant checks.

## Why This Change Was Made

The three Periphery scope jobs now compare GitHub's synthetic pull-request merge commit with its first parent, which is the exact base tree used to build that merge result. Checkout depth is increased to two so both commits are available; the stale event-base fetch is no longer needed.

Scope behavior remains fail-closed, manual dispatch still scans, draft pull requests still skip, and renamed files remain covered.

## User Impact

Unrelated pull requests no longer start iOS, macOS, or shared OpenClawKit Periphery scan jobs solely because `main` changed. Pull requests that actually touch the scoped native paths continue to run the same scans.

AI-assisted change; I reviewed and understand the implementation and tests.

target.title: docs: respect configured Crabbox provider for agent tests
target.body:
Related: #104485

## What Problem This Solves

Ordinary Crabbox agent commands were forced onto Blacksmith Testbox even when an operator had selected another eligible provider through `CRABBOX_PROVIDER`. That made machine-local provider preferences ineffective and could also cause local-container execution to be described as remote/Testbox proof.

## Why This Change Was Made

Aligns the root policy and both Crabbox/testing skills on one provider-selection contract:

1. Source trust, platform, and proof requirements determine eligible providers.
2. An explicit eligible provider requested by the user wins.
3. Ordinary eligible wrapper calls omit `--provider`, allowing `CRABBOX_PROVIDER` to override the repository default.
4. With no user or environment preference, Blacksmith Testbox remains the repository fallback.

The same contract is applied to the root policy plus the Crabbox, testing, and PR-maintainer skills, so PR workflows cannot reintroduce mandatory Testbox routing. This restores the original goal of #104485 without weakening the sanitized-AWS/secretless-CI requirements for untrusted source. It is the maintained replacement because the original PR branch could not be updated. Original contributor: @hxy91819.

## User Impact

Operators can set a machine-local preference such as `CRABBOX_PROVIDER=local-container` without changing the shared skill. AWS or another eligible provider can be selected the same way. Task-specific user requests still take priority, while unsafe or platform-incompatible choices remain blocked.

## Evidence

- Current head: `32452922d779597437621cdf63fb02d740b49837`.
- Dependency contract checked in Crabbox source: config files load before environment overrides, `CRABBOX_PROVIDER` overrides the configured provider, and an explicit CLI `--provider` remains the final override.
- Claude via acpx independently routed the policy cases correctly: env `local-container` -> local Docker proof with no explicit provider; unset env -> Blacksmith fallback; untrusted credential-hydrated Testbox request -> sanitized AWS or secretless CI.

target.title: fix(memory-lancedb): make table initialization atomic
target.body:
Closes #105680

## What Problem This Solves

The bundled LanceDB memory plugin checked whether the `memories` table existed and then created it in a separate operation. Two OpenClaw processes initializing the same database could both observe the table as absent, race during creation, and fail startup with a duplicate-create error.

## Why This Change Was Made

Keep the existing fast path for an already-present table, but make the absent-table path use the LanceDB 0.30.0 atomic `existOk` create mode. This keeps concurrency ownership in the database dependency, avoids a filesystem lock that would not fit remote storage URIs, and keeps schema-row cleanup idempotent.

The regression test starts six independent Node processes against one fresh LanceDB directory and requires every process to complete initialization successfully. The same scenario fails against the previous implementation.

LanceDB documents that `existOk: true` suppresses the existing-table error in create mode and ignores the losing caller supplied data: https://lancedb.github.io/lancedb/js/interfaces/CreateTableOptions/

## User Impact

Gateway and worker processes can initialize the same memory-lancedb store concurrently without intermittent duplicate-create startup failures.

## Evidence

Final-head validation:

- Candidate head: `4e1bc84e3e1`; rebased onto `origin/main` at `652266b8b6c`.
- Production diff after the current TypeScript LOC ratchet: `12 additions / 13 deletions`; the legacy production file no longer grows.

### Standalone concurrent-process behavior proof

Environment: macOS arm64, Node 24.15.0, exact `@lancedb/lancedb@0.30.0`, one fresh temporary local LanceDB directory. This proof ran outside Vitest. The temporary driver started six independent Node processes; each imported the production `extensions/memory-lancedb/index.ts` module and called `testing.createMemoryDb(dbPath, 4).count()`.

Pre-fix control: the same final-head snapshot with only `{ existOk: true }` removed while retaining the test access hook:

```text
initializer 2: failed (1)
initializer 3: failed (1)
initializer 4: failed (1)
initializer 5: failed (1)
initializer 1: failed (1)
initializer 6: ok
Error: Table memories already exists
before_exit=1
```

Final head:

```text
initializer 5: ok
initializer 1: ok
initializer 3: ok
initializer 6: ok
initializer 4: ok
initializer 2: ok
tables: memories
rows: 0
after_exit=0
```

The final table is usable, all six initializers return successfully, and the temporary schema row is removed.

### Tests and gates

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/memory-lancedb/index.test.ts extensions/memory-lancedb/memory-lancedb.concurrent.test.ts` under Node 24.15.0 — 2 files and 126 tests passed.
- `check:changed` passed conflict markers, the TypeScript LOC ratchet, attributions, extension export guards, duplicate coverage, dependency pins, and formatting. Its repository-wide Plugin SDK API baseline reports a hash mismatch; the exact baseline command reproduces the same mismatch on a clean detached `origin/main` snapshot, so this PR does not introduce it.
- `git diff --check origin/main...HEAD` — passed.
- Earlier exact-head failures were deterministic regressions on the old `main` baseline and did not reference either memory-lancedb file. The current `main` repair at [`2c95bd2387c`](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/commit/2c95bd2387cdcfab5b3736f3ab6d08a4ad23cb65) is included; fresh exact-head CI run [29386264145](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29386264145) passed with 46 checks green, including `openclaw/ci-gate`.

Remote Testbox delegation was unavailable because the installed Crabbox binary is 0.16.0 while the current flow requires 0.22.0 or newer. The proof above is secretless local execution, and GitHub CI remains the remote verification lane.

target.title: fix(cli): one-shot agent --local runs never export OTel diagnostics
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where one-shot `openclaw agent --local` runs would export no OTel telemetry at all when `diagnostics.otel.enabled: true` and the `diagnostics-otel` plugin are configured: zero spans, metrics, or logs reached the OTLP collector, while the same turns dispatched through the Gateway exported fine. Gateway-to-embedded fallback runs (gateway timeout or transport failure) silently dropped telemetry the same way, so exactly the runs that bypass the Gateway were invisible in tracing backends.

## Why This Change Was Made

Diagnostics exporters are plugin services and were only ever started inside the Gateway process (`startPluginServices` at gateway startup/reload); embedded CLI runs emit diagnostic events in the CLI process where nothing subscribes. The CLI now starts the `diagnostics-otel` service around embedded agent runs via a scoped, non-activating plugin load that honors the same plugin-enablement config as the Gateway, and flushes on exit: drain the async diagnostic-event queue, then shut the SDK down (force flush), bounded by a 10s timeout so an unreachable collector cannot hang the CLI. `diagnostics-prometheus` intentionally stays Gateway-only — it is a pull-based scrape server that is useless in a short-lived process and would race the Gateway for its port. No new config surface; configs without OTel enabled short-circuit before any plugin load.

## User Impact

Operators running one-shot `openclaw agent --local` turns (and runs that fall back from the Gateway to the embedded agent) now get the same OTel traces, metrics, and logs as Gateway-executed turns, flushed before the process exits. Setups without OTel export enabled are unaffected.

## Evidence

- Live before/after on macOS against a local Arize Phoenix OTLP collector: before, one-shot `--local` runs produced zero spans while Gateway runs exported fine; after, a one-shot run logs `diagnostics-otel: logs exporter enabled (OTLP/Protobuf)` and `openclaw.harness.run`, `openclaw.run`, and `openclaw.model.call` spans (with `gen_ai.*` attributes) arrive in Phoenix seconds after the process exits.
- New focused tests: `src/plugins/one-shot-diagnostics.test.ts` covers config gating (no plugin load when OTel is off), the scoped non-activating load, exporter allowlist filtering, drain-before-stop ordering, and the flush timeout bound; `src/commands/agent-via-gateway.test.ts` adds cases for start/flush ordering around local runs, flush when the embedded run fails, run survival when exporter startup fails, exporter start on gateway-to-embedded fallback, and no exporter on Gateway dispatch. Both files pass (9 + 73 tests) rebased on current `main`.
- `pnpm build` clean with no `[INEFFECTIVE_DYNAMIC_IMPORT]` warnings; `tsgo` core and test lanes clean; oxfmt/oxlint clean on touched files. Validation ran locally via `scripts/run-vitest.mjs` (remote Testbox was unavailable in this environment).

## Summary

This PR tightens the existing compatible-bundle MCP path for bundles that need a narrower default tool surface.

- Adds regression coverage that a Codex-compatible bundle `.mcp.json` preserves `toolFilter.include`, `toolFilter.exclude`, and a relative bundle data root.
- Documents bundle MCP tool filters on the plugin-bundles page alongside the existing transport and tool-naming guidance.
- Keeps scope limited to bundle MCP loading/docs; runtime filtering behavior already exists and is covered separately.

Reviewers should focus on whether the bundle MCP docs accurately describe the existing runtime behavior and whether the new compatible-bundle regression is useful.

## Linked context

No issue filed.

Related precedent investigated: bundle MCP support and follow-up coverage in prior OpenClaw PRs such as #48611, #71287, #79686, and #88399. This PR follows that existing bundle MCP seam.

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

Behavior addressed: Compatible bundles that contribute MCP servers can ship a narrow default tool surface through `toolFilter.include` and `toolFilter.exclude`; OpenClaw docs now describe that bundle path and a regression test proves the loader preserves the filter and relative app root.

Real environment tested: Local OpenClaw checkout on macOS, branch `test/filtered-bundle-mcp`, commit `d5bffb3dc0`, with an isolated temporary `HOME`, `OPENCLAW_HOME`, and `OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`.

Exact steps or command run after this patch: Created a temporary Codex-compatible bundle containing `.codex-plugin/plugin.json`, `.mcp.json`, `skills/`, and `apps/`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins install --link <temp>/vision-mcp`; ran `pnpm openclaw plugins inspect vision-mcp --json`; then loaded bundle MCP config with `node --import tsx` calling `loadEnabledBundleMcpConfig(...)` against the isolated home/config.

Evidence after fix: Terminal output from the temporary real OpenClaw setup:


Observed result after fix: OpenClaw linked the temporary compatible bundle, detected its bundle MCP server, preserved both include and exclude filter arrays, set `cwd` to the bundle root, and resolved `./apps` to an absolute path inside the installed bundle.

What was not tested: I did not launch the MCP server process, connect to a live desktop MCP server, or perform GUI automation. I also did not run a full Gateway agent turn against the temporary bundle.

Proof limitations or environment constraints: The proof uses a temporary local compatible bundle and the real OpenClaw plugin installer/loader, but the MCP server command itself is not started because this PR changes documentation and loader regression coverage, not MCP runtime execution behavior.

## Tests and validation

Commands run:

```text
node scripts/test-projects.mjs -- src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts --reporter=verbose
pnpm format:check src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts
git diff --check
pnpm check:docs
codex review --base origin/main
```

Regression coverage added: `src/plugins/bundle-mcp.test.ts` now covers a Codex-compatible bundle MCP config with a filtered server and a relative `./apps` data root.

Validation results:

```text

codex review --base origin/main: No actionable correctness issues were found
```

## Risk checklist

Did user-visible behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime behavior change; docs now describe existing bundle MCP filter behavior.

Did config, environment, or migration behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No.

Did security, auth, secrets, network, or tool execution behavior change? (`Yes/No`): No runtime change. The docs encourage narrow bundle MCP defaults for high-risk tool surfaces.

What is the highest-risk area? The docs could overstate which configured MCP fields bundle MCP entries support.

How is that risk mitigated? Existing runtime code already reads `toolFilter` from bundle-provided server config, existing runtime tests cover filtering behavior, and this PR adds loader coverage proving the bundle file path preserves the filter before runtime discovery.

AI-assisted: yes.

Next action: maintainer review.

## Summary

- Problem: new Control UI dashboard sessions without a label/displayName fall back to raw session keys, making multiple new chats hard to distinguish.
- Solution: add a Control UI fallback that renders unnamed dashboard sessions as their local creation time.
- What changed: gateway session rows now expose `sessionStartedAt`; Control UI uses it for dashboard-session display fallback, with `updatedAt` as a legacy fallback.
- What did NOT change (scope boundary): no persisted labels are written, no rename UI was added, and explicit labels/display names still win.

AI-assisted: yes. I used a local coding agent and ran the verification below myself.

## Motivation

- Closes #86040.
- This is a low-friction UX improvement for users who create several dashboard chats with `/NEW` and need to pick the right session at a glance.

## Change Type (select all)

- [ ] Bug fix
- [x] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [x] API / contracts
- [x] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Closes #86040
- [ ] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Real behavior proof (required for external PRs)

- Behavior or issue addressed: unnamed Control UI dashboard sessions now display a local timestamp fallback instead of the raw `agent:<id>:dashboard:<uuid>` key, while named sessions still display their explicit label.
- Real environment tested: macOS 26.5 (25F71), local OpenClaw checkout at this PR branch, Node v23.11.0, pnpm 11.2.2.
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:
  - `pnpm --dir ui exec tsx -e "import { resolveSessionDisplayName } from './src/ui/session-display.ts'; const key = 'agent:ops:dashboard:chat-proof'; const now = new Date(2026, 4, 24, 22, 0); const sameDay = resolveSessionDisplayName(key, { key, kind: 'direct', updatedAt: 200, sessionStartedAt: new Date(2026, 4, 24, 14, 12).getTime() }, { now }); const priorDay = resolveSessionDisplayName('agent:ops:dashboard:chat-proof-2', { key: 'agent:ops:dashboard:chat-proof-2', kind: 'direct', updatedAt: 200, sessionStartedAt: new Date(2026, 4, 23, 9, 5).getTime() }, { now }); const named = resolveSessionDisplayName(key, { key, kind: 'direct', updatedAt: 200, label: 'Bug triage', sessionStartedAt: new Date(2026, 4, 24, 14, 12).getTime() }, { now }); console.log(JSON.stringify({ sameDay, priorDay, named }, null, 2));"`
- Evidence after fix (screenshot, recording, terminal capture, console output, redacted runtime log, linked artifact, or copied live output):

```json
{
  "sameDay": "14:12",
  "priorDay": "05-23 09:05",
  "named": "Bug triage"
}
```

- Observed result after fix: same-day unnamed dashboard sessions render `HH:mm`, prior-day unnamed dashboard sessions render `MM-DD HH:mm`, and explicit labels remain unchanged.
- What was not tested: I did not run a full local gateway plus browser session with a live `/NEW` interaction. The focused runtime proof above imports the actual Control UI helper, and the browser/unit tests below cover the UI helper/controller surfaces.
- Before evidence (optional but encouraged): the new RED test initially failed with `expected 'agent:ops:dashboard:chat-1' to be '14:12'` before the implementation.

## Root Cause (if applicable)

- Root cause: N/A, this is a feature request.
- Missing detection / guardrail: unnamed dashboard-session display fallback was not covered.

- Coverage level that should have caught this:
  - [x] Unit test
  - [x] Seam / integration test
  - [ ] End-to-end test
  - [ ] Existing coverage already sufficient
- Target test or file: `ui/src/ui/app-render.helpers.node.test.ts` and `src/gateway/session-utils.test.ts`.
- Scenario the test should lock in: unnamed dashboard sessions use `sessionStartedAt` for timestamp fallback; explicit labels still win; gateway rows include `sessionStartedAt`.

```text
Before:
/NEW -> agent:ops:dashboard:<uuid> -> raw key shown when unlabeled

After:
```

## Summary
- The runtime already walks `memory/` recursively via `collectMemoryFilesFromDir` (`packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/internal.ts`), so nested files like `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md` are indexed and searched. But several agent-facing descriptors and public docs still said `memory/*.md`, which can mislead agents into thinking the index is flat.
- This PR updates the remaining stale references to `memory/**/*.md`. No runtime behavior change.

## Files touched
- `extensions/memory-core/index.ts` — lazy `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptors
- `extensions/memory-core/src/tools.ts` — concrete `memory_search` / `memory_get` descriptions
- `extensions/memory-core/src/prompt-section.ts` — system-prompt recall guidance
- `src/config/schema.help.ts` — `agents.defaults.memorySearch` help text
- `docs/concepts/memory-builtin.md`, `memory.md`, `system-prompt.md`
- `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/reference/token-use.md`
- `docs/.generated/config-baseline.sha256` regenerated via `pnpm config:docs:gen`

## Note
This supersedes #72748. That PR also carried QMD watcher changes that were independently resolved upstream by #81802 (`watch-settle.ts`), so the surviving value was just this wording alignment. Splitting it out as a small, behavior-neutral PR for easier review.

## Real behavior proof

**Behavior or issue addressed**: Agent-facing descriptors and public docs said `memory/*.md` even though the runtime already walks `memory/` recursively and indexes nested files such as `memory/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.md`. This PR aligns the wording to `memory/**/*.md` so agents and readers see what is actually indexed. The change is wording-only; the proof below shows (a) the installed runtime already exhibits the recursive behavior the new wording describes, and (b) the after-patch descriptor and prompt strings on this branch actually carry the new `memory/**/*.md` wording when imported at runtime.

**Real environment tested**: Installed OpenClaw `2026.5.20` (npm global, current `latest` published build, ahead of the `acf265d` base this PR branches from), against the live workspace `~/.openclaw/workspace-moku` used by the gateway. target.title: [codex] Fix Anthropic Vertex npm audit regression
target.body:
## Summary

- remove the `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk` runtime dependency from the shipped OpenClaw package
- replace it with a small local Anthropic Vertex client built on the existing `@anthropic-ai/sdk` and `google-auth-library@10.6.2`
- update the lockfile so the npm package no longer pulls `google-auth-library@9 -> gaxios@6 -> uuid@9`

## Why

`openclaw@2026.5.2-beta.1` introduced a clean npm audit regression for consumers: `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk@0.16.0` depends on `google-auth-library@^9.4.2`, which resolves to `gaxios@6.7.1` and `uuid@9.0.1`. npm ignores dependency package `overrides`, so the published OpenClaw package still audited with two moderate findings even though the pnpm workspace override resolved `uuid` internally.

## Validation

- `pnpm tsgo:extensions`
- `pnpm exec vitest run extensions/anthropic-vertex`
- `pnpm exec oxlint extensions/anthropic-vertex/stream-runtime.ts`
- `pnpm audit --prod --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- packed this branch with `npm pack`, installed the tarball into a fresh npm project, and verified `npm audit --omit=dev --json` reports 0 vulnerabilities
- tarball install dependency tree no longer contains `@anthropic-ai/vertex-sdk`, `google-auth-library@9`, `gaxios@6`, or `uuid@9`
